68	**Abstract**
69	
70	Anchors bias numeric estimates, but it is unclear whether an anchor's proportional influence rises, stays constant or falls as the anchor becomes more extreme. Meta-analyses report larger standardised effects for more distant anchors, yet a standardised mean difference rises with anchor distance even when the proportional pull is constant. We derived the shape of the anchor-response function from five process models (anchor-and-adjust with a fixed or a resource-rational number of adjustments, constant-weight integration, adjustment to the edge of the plausible range, and plausibility-discounted integration), simulated them on the designs of the Open Anchoring Quest, and preregistered the predictions before reading any estimates. In `r dc$within_cells` item-study cells with at least three anchor values (`r nf(P$n_rows)` estimates, mostly random anchors), the log-scale elasticity of estimates with respect to anchors averaged `r f2(P$b)` and fell as anchors moved away from the true value (curvature `r f3(P$g)`, 95% CI `r ci(P$g_lo, P$g_hi)`; relative curvature `r f2(P$rho)`). This contradicts anchor-and-adjust with a fixed number of adjustments and constant-weight integration. Across `r h2$n_cells` two-anchor cells from `r h2$n_studies` studies, the anchoring index did not change detectably with extremity (slope `r f3(h2$slope)`, `r ci(h2$slope_lo, h2$slope_hi)`). Only the resource-rational variant, whose predictions were least constrained, survived the preregistered model checks. Proportional anchor influence declines within items, whereas comparisons across items with researcher-chosen anchors do not show this decline.
71	
72	**Keywords:** anchoring, anchor extremity, process models, resource rationality, secondary data analysis, preregistration
73	
74	# Introduction
75	
76	Numeric judgements are drawn towards numbers people have just considered. In the classic demonstration, participants who first judged whether the percentage of African countries in the United Nations was higher or lower than a random number gave estimates that moved towards that number [@tversky1974]. The effect appears with arbitrary and informative anchors, with lay people and experts, and in consequential settings such as property valuation and criminal sentencing [@northcraft1987; @englich2006; @furnham2011]. A meta-analysis of openly shared trial-level data from 90 anchoring studies estimated a pooled standardised effect of *g* = 0.69 [@roseler2022meta; @roseler2022opaq].
77	
78	Whether an anchor's influence depends on how extreme it is has practical and theoretical weight. Practically, negotiators, litigants and survey designers choose anchor values, and whether an extreme opening offer buys proportionally more influence than a moderate one depends on this relation. Theoretically, the leading accounts of anchoring make different predictions about this question, so the shape of the relation between anchor extremity and anchor influence is one of the few places where they can be tested against each other.
79	
80	## Evidence on anchor extremity
81	
82	Experiments that varied anchor extremity have produced mixed results. @chapman1994 found that "implausibly extreme anchors had a proportionally smaller effect than anchors close to the expected value" in lottery valuations. @strack1997 found that implausible anchors produced a larger raw shift in estimates than plausible ones. When implausible anchors were placed far beyond the plausible range, estimates under them were no higher than estimates under a plausible high anchor [@mussweiler2001], and @wegener2001 found that very extreme anchors had smaller effects than moderate ones. These studies compared two to four anchor levels, mostly for a handful of items.
83	
84	The two recent meta-analyses reach different conclusions. Using the Open Anchoring Quest (OpAQ) data, @roseler2022meta found that Hedges' *g* increased with the relative distance between anchor and true value and concluded against the prediction that extreme anchors produce smaller effects. @schley2026 coded extremity as a binary flag for anchors that the original authors described as extreme and found no difference in effect size. @barrera2024 modelled the anchored crowd mean as a weighted average of anchor and crowd mean, with a weight that decays exponentially with the distance between anchor and truth, and found that this weight fell with distance across 30 percentage questions.
85	
86	These results are hard to compare because they measure anchor influence in different units. A standardised mean difference between high- and low-anchor conditions rises with the distance between the anchors even if every anchor pulls estimates by the same proportion of its distance. A finding that *g* grows with anchor distance is therefore compatible with constant, rising and falling proportional influence. The theories speak to the proportional pull: how much of the distance between belief and anchor is carried into the estimate. @jacowitz1995 captured this with the anchoring index, the difference between median estimates under high and low anchors divided by the difference between the anchors, and @roseler2022meta called for such a unitless measure "to formalize the relationship between anchor distance and adjustment strength".
87	
88	## Process models and their predictions
89	
90	We consider five process models. Each maps an anchor and a belief onto an estimate, and each implies a shape for the relation between anchor extremity and proportional pull ([@fig-models]).
91	
92	In *anchor-and-adjust with a fixed number of adjustments* (M1), people start at the anchor and adjust towards their belief in a limited number of stochastic steps. @lieder2018a formalised adjustment as a Metropolis-Hastings chain that starts at the anchor and moves towards the belief distribution. When the anchor is far away, each step covers a bounded distance, so a fixed number of steps leaves a larger share of the distance uncorrected, and the proportional pull rises with extremity. Lieder et al. approximated the chain's convergence as geometric, which implies a constant proportional pull (their Eq. 4); that approximation holds for anchors near the belief, and our simulations use the chain itself.
93	
94	In *resource-rational anchor-and-adjust* (M1R), the number of adjustments is chosen to minimise expected error plus a time cost per adjustment [@lieder2018a, Eq. 2]. Anchors inside the plausible range are barely adjusted, because adjusting from them buys little accuracy, while far anchors justify many adjustments. The resulting pull can fall with extremity, but its shape depends on the time cost and on how uncertain people are.
95	
96	In *constant-weight integration* (M2), the estimate is a weighted average of anchor and belief with a fixed weight. This is the simplest version of the anchor integration model [@turner2016], and in log units it implies a constant proportional pull. It is the null model for shape.
97	
98	In *adjustment to the plausible boundary* (M3), people accept anchors that lie inside the range of values they find plausible and adjust from implausible anchors only until they reach the edge of that range [@epley2006]. Beyond the boundary the estimate stops moving, so the proportional pull falls towards zero.
99	
100	In *plausibility-discounted integration* (M4), the anchor's weight declines as the anchor becomes implausible. This formalises the proposal that extreme anchors lose influence because they are implausible [@wegener2001], and it resembles the anchor integration model, in which an anchor's influence depends on how consistent it is with prior beliefs [@turner2016]. Selective-accessibility accounts, in which anchoring arises from anchor-consistent knowledge activated during the comparison [@strack1997; @mussweiler1999], have been read as predicting smaller effects for implausible anchors [@roseler2022meta]. The pull falls, and far enough out, a more extreme anchor moves the estimate back towards the belief.
101	
102	```{r fig-models}
103	#| fig-cap: "Model predictions at the median calibrated parameter values. (A) Mean log estimate relative to the belief centre as a function of the anchor's distance from the belief centre, in units of belief uncertainty. (B) Local elasticity, the proportional pull of the anchor. M1: anchor-and-adjust with a fixed number of adjustments; M1R: resource-rational anchor-and-adjust; M2: constant-weight integration; M3: adjustment to the plausible boundary; M4: plausibility-discounted integration."
104	knitr::include_graphics(here("manuscript", "figures", "fig1_model_predictions.png"))
105	```
106	
107	The models also include a no-anchoring baseline (M0). Lieder et al. derived that bias grows linearly with anchor distance when the number of adjustments is fixed and showed how the optimal number of adjustments depends on distance, but did not test how the anchoring index varies with extremity. @turner2016 built an inverted U between extremity and anchor influence into their model "for simplicity" and tested it with one anchor per item.
108	
109	## The present study
110	
111	We tested these predictions on OpAQ, an openly licensed collection of trial-level anchoring data [@roseler2022opaq]. Because anchor values in most studies were chosen by the original authors together with the items, a comparison across items confounds extremity with item properties. Our primary test is therefore within items: in studies that presented many different anchors for the same question, we asked how the proportional pull changes as the anchor moves away from the true value. A comparison of the anchoring index across two-anchor studies is a secondary test. We simulated every model on the exact OpAQ designs to derive numeric predictions and passed the simulated data through the same estimators as the observed data. We preregistered the predictions, decision rules and analyses before reading any estimate.
112	
113	# Method
114	
115	## Transparency and openness
116	
117	The preregistration (following the secondary-data template of @vandenakker2021), the frozen model predictions, all code and all outputs are in the project repository. The preregistration was committed to version control before the estimates were read; a reader function refuses to load the outcome column unless the preregistration is committed. The one-command script `run_all.sh` reproduces every number from the raw data. Four deviations from the preregistration are listed in the section on deviations below. The study was designed, coded, analysed and written by an AI system under the instruction of the author; the declarations at the end describe this in detail.
118	
119	## Data
120	
121	OpAQ [@roseler2022opaq; @opaqosf] aggregates openly available and contributed anchoring datasets into one trial-level file with harmonised design codes. We used the newest version of the file (`opaq_70a.csv`, dated 10 February 2023), which contains `r nf(dc$opaq_rows)` estimates from `r dc$opaq_studies` studies and `r dc$opaq_items` items. It is licensed under CC-BY 4.0 and contains no personal identifiers beyond sex, age and nationality, none of which we used.
122	
123	Estimates entered the analysis if the anchor was explicitly random, fixed, or relevant to the target (self-generated and incidental anchors were excluded); the response scale was open; the quantity was a positive ratio-scale magnitude (e.g., a length, price, population or count, but not a date, temperature, percentage or preference); and anchor and true value were positive. We excluded one study whose anchors were computed from each participant's own unanchored estimates. Two sets were formed from these estimates.
124	
125	- **Within-item set** (primary): item-study cells with at least three distinct anchor values. It contains `r dc$within_cells` cells from `r dc$within_studies` studies (`r nf(dc$within_rows)` estimates, `r nf(dc$within_participants)` participants). Fifteen cells used random anchors: 13 general-knowledge items from @bahnik2021, in which each participant compared 13 random anchors between 1 and 1,000 to 13 lengths and heights, and two items from @yoon2021. Five cells used fixed anchors: four items with 10 high anchor levels each from unpublished data by Frech et al. (2021) and one item with 20 anchor levels from unpublished data by Imhoff and Barker (2022), both contributed to OpAQ.
126	- **Across-cell set** (secondary): cells with fixed or relevant anchors, exactly one low and one high anchor value, a log ratio of at least 0.25 between them, and at least 10 estimates per anchor. It contains `r dc$across_cells` cells from `r dc$across_studies` studies (`r nf(dc$across_rows)` estimates).
127	
128	## Measures
129	
130	For every estimate we computed *y* = ln(estimate / true value) and *x* = ln(anchor / true value). Working on the log scale treats a doubling of a height and a doubling of a population alike and matches the roughly log-normal spread of numeric estimates. The log elasticity, the change in *y* per unit change in *x*, is a unitless proportional pull: an elasticity of .5 means that doubling the anchor multiplies the estimate by about 1.41.
131	
132	In the within-item set we modelled *y* = *a*~cell~ + *b*·*x* + *g*·*x*|*x*|. Here *b* is the average elasticity at the true value, and the curvature *g* describes how the local elasticity (*b* + 2*g*|*x*|) changes as the anchor moves away from the true value in either direction. We also report the relative curvature ρ = *g*/*b*, which does not depend on the overall strength of anchoring. In the across-cell set we computed each cell's log anchoring index, the difference between the median *y* under the high and the low anchor divided by the log ratio of the anchors, and each cell's extremity, the mean absolute log distance of its two anchors from the true value.
133	
134	## Model predictions
135	
136	The five process models and the no-anchoring baseline were implemented on the log scale ([@fig-models]; specification in `R/models.R`). Every participant-item combination had a belief centre drawn around the true value, with item-level bias and between-person spread. Responses included response noise and a 2% share of gross errors. Model parameters are expressed in units of the item's belief uncertainty σ, which was drawn from 0.3 to 1.2 log units per item.
137	
138	To fix the models' parameters without using OpAQ outcomes, we calibrated each model to the anchoring index that @jacowitz1995 reported for anchors at the 15th and 85th percentiles of unanchored estimates (about .49), accepting parameter values that produced an index between .30 and .60. The preregistered calibration computed this index on the log scale; a raw-scale recalibration is reported as a sensitivity analysis. The number of accepted grid points per model was `r paste(sprintf("%s: %d", acc$model, acc$N), collapse = "; ")`. We then simulated each model on the exact OpAQ designs (the same anchors, true values, participants and cell sizes; `r n_rep[model == "M0"]$N` replicates for M0 and `r n_rep[model == "M1"]$N` for each other model), drawing parameters from the accepted set, and passed each simulated dataset through the estimators used for the observed data. [@tbl-predictions] lists the resulting predictions.
139	
140	```{r tbl-predictions}
141	#| tbl-cap: "Preregistered model predictions: medians and 95% predictive intervals across simulated replicates."
142	q <- function(v) sprintf("%.3f [%.3f, %.3f]", median(v), quantile(v, .025), quantile(v, .975))
143	tab <- pred[, .(`Average elasticity b` = q(b), `Curvature g` = q(g),
144	                `Relative curvature ρ` = if (.BY$Model == "M0") "—" else q(rho),
145	                `Across-cell slope d` = q(across_slope)), by = .(Model = model)]
146	tab[, Model := c(M0 = "M0 No anchoring", M1 = "M1 Anchor-and-adjust, fixed", M1R = "M1R Anchor-and-adjust, resource-rational",
147	                 M2 = "M2 Constant weight", M3 = "M3 Plausible boundary", M4 = "M4 Plausibility discount")[Model]]
148	knitr::kable(tab)
149	```
150	
151	The predictions separate the models by shape. M1 predicts positive curvature (median *g* = `r f3(med_("M1", "g"))`), M2 zero curvature, and M3 and M4 negative curvature (`r f3(med_("M3", "g"))` and `r f3(med_("M4", "g"))`). M1R's curvature depends on its parameters, with a predictive interval spanning zero. The across-cell slope follows the same pattern.
152	
153	## Analysis plan
154	
155	**H1 (primary).** In the within-item set we fitted a linear mixed model with fixed effects for *x* and *x*|*x*|, uncorrelated random intercepts, slopes and curvatures by cell, and random intercepts by participant, using lme4 and lmerTest [@bates2015; @kuznetsova2017] in R [@rcore2026]. Confidence intervals for *b* and *g* used Satterthwaite degrees of freedom; the interval for ρ used a delta-method standard error. Estimates were removed as gross errors when their log distance from the true value exceeded both ln(1000) and the cell's largest anchor distance plus ln(10), a rule that never removes a response equal to an anchor. H1a and H1b applied the same model to the random-anchor and fixed-anchor strata.
156	
157	**Decision rules.** The shape test was interpreted only if the confidence interval for *b* lay above zero (gate G1). We then classified the curvature, in this order, as *flat* if the confidence interval for ρ lay within the equivalence bounds ±0.05, as *rising* if the interval for *g* lay above zero, as *falling* if it lay below zero, and otherwise as inconclusive. The bounds sit just below the smallest relative curvature in the 95% predictive interval of M1, M3 and M4 and far outside that of M2 [@lakens2017]. Applied to the simulated replicates, this rule labelled data generated by M1 as rising in more than 99% of replicates, data from M3 and M4 as falling in more than 99%, data from M2 as flat in more than 99%, and data from M0 as failing the gate in all replicates.
158	
159	**H2 (secondary).** We regressed the cell-level log anchoring index on extremity in a multilevel meta-regression with random intercepts for studies and cells within studies [@viechtbauer2010], using standard errors derived from the median absolute deviation (MAD) of each condition. Gate G2 required the mean index to exceed zero; the slope *d* was classified with the same ordered rule and equivalence bounds of ±0.03.
160	
161	**H3 (model adequacy).** A model was contradicted when the observed curvature (*g* or ρ) or the across-cell slope *d* fell outside its 95% predictive interval; M0 was also contradicted if gate G1 passed. The observed level of anchoring (*b* and the mean index) was compared with each model's interval but did not decide survival, because levels inherit the calibration to Jacowitz and Kahneman's design.
162	
163	**Robustness.** We preregistered seven robustness analyses: median regression without the gross-error rule, with a participant-cluster bootstrap [@koenker1978; @quantreg]; separate slopes for near (|*x*| ≤ 1) and far anchors; H1 without @bahnik2021; H2 with the raw-scale anchoring index; H2 with design covariates; H2 without one study flagged by a later correction; and two alternative extremity measures.
164	
165	## Deviations from the preregistration
166	
167	We made four changes after the confirmatory analysis had been run. First, a code review found that the observed mean anchoring index in the H3 level check was computed with a different estimator from the simulated one; we replaced it with the same inverse-variance weighted mean. This affects only level criteria, which do not decide model survival. Second, the preregistration described one M1R parameter incorrectly; the code, and therefore the predictions, were correct. Third, we made code changes that altered no reported number. Fourth, we clarified that the relative-curvature interval uses a normal critical value. One cell was removed by the preregistered gross-error rule because its participants answered in millions while its anchors and true value were raw counts. All analyses labelled exploratory or sensitivity were added after the preregistration.
168	
169	# Results
170	
171	After exclusions the within-item analysis included `r nf(P$n_rows)` estimates in `r P$n_cells` cells (`r excl[set == "within"]$invalid_estimate` estimates were missing or non-positive; no gross errors). The across-cell analysis included `r h2$n_cells` cells and `r nf(h2$n_rows)` estimates; `r nf(excl[set == "across"]$invalid_estimate)` estimates were missing or non-positive and `r nf(excl[set == "across"]$gross_error)` were removed as gross errors, `r nf(870)` of them from the cell with the unit mismatch.
172	
173	## Within items, the proportional pull falls with extremity (H1)
174	
175	Anchoring was clearly present in the within-item set: the average elasticity was *b* = `r f3(P$b)`, 95% CI `r ci(P$b_lo, P$b_hi)`, so doubling the anchor raised estimates by about `r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * (2^P$b - 1))` near the true value. The curvature was negative, *g* = `r f3(P$g)`, `r ci(P$g_lo, P$g_hi)`, *t*(`r f2(P$g_df, 1)`) = `r f2(P$g / ((P$g_hi - P$g_lo) / (2 * qt(.975, P$g_df))))`, *p* `r if (P$g_p < .001) "< .001" else paste("=", sprintf("%.3f", P$g_p))`, with a relative curvature of ρ = `r f2(P$rho)`, `r ci(P$rho_lo, P$rho_hi, 2)`. By the preregistered rule, the elasticity *falls* with extremity. At the true value an anchor carried about `r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * P$b)` of its log distance into the estimate. The fitted local elasticity *b* + 2*g*|*x*| was `r f2(loc_el(1))` for anchors one log unit (a factor of 2.7) from the true value and `r f2(loc_el(2))` for anchors two log units (a factor of 7.4) away, about half its value at the true value. [@fig-within] shows the binned observed estimates and the fitted curves for each cell.
176	
177	In the random-anchor stratum the result was the same: *b* = `r f3(R$b)`, `r ci(R$b_lo, R$b_hi)`, and *g* = `r f3(R$g)`, `r ci(R$g_lo, R$g_hi)`, again classified as falling. In the fixed-anchor stratum the point estimates were similar (*b* = `r f3(FX$b)`, *g* = `r f3(FX$g)`, `r ci(FX$g_lo, FX$g_hi)`), but with only five cells the confidence interval for *b* spanned `r ci(FX$b_lo, FX$b_hi, 2)`, so the gate failed and the shape was not testable there under the preregistered rules.
178	
179	```{r fig-within}
180	#| fig-cap: "Observed within-item response functions. Points are median log estimates in 0.5-unit bins of the log anchor (bins with at least 10 estimates), connected within each item. Blue curves are the fitted H1 model for each item (fixed plus item-level random effects), drawn over the central 95% of that item's anchors. The dashed line marks estimates equal to the anchor. Axes differ between panels."
181	knitr::include_graphics(here("manuscript", "figures", "fig2_within_item.png"))
182	```
183	
184	## Across cells, the anchoring index shows no clear trend (H2)
185	
186	Anchoring was present across cells: the mean log anchoring index was `r f2(h2$mean_ai)`, `r ci(h2$mean_ai_lo, h2$mean_ai_hi, 2)`. The slope of the index on extremity was *d* = `r f3(h2$slope)`, `r ci(h2$slope_lo, h2$slope_hi)`. This interval includes zero but is not narrow enough to establish equivalence within ±0.03, so the result is inconclusive under the preregistered rule ([@fig-across], panel A). The point estimate is positive, the opposite sign to the within-item curvature.
187	
188	```{r fig-across}
189	#| fig-cap: "Across-cell relation between anchor extremity and anchor influence. (A) Log anchoring index per cell with the preregistered meta-regression line and 95% confidence band. (B) Hedges' *g* per cell (exploratory). Point area is proportional to precision (1/SE). The standardised effect rises with extremity, while the proportional index does not change detectably."
190	knitr::include_graphics(here("manuscript", "figures", "fig3_across_cells.png"))
191	```
192	
193	## Model adequacy (H3)
194	
195	[@tbl-h3] compares the observed statistics with each model's predictive interval. M1 predicts positive curvature and is contradicted by the negative observed curvature. M2 predicts no curvature and is contradicted as well. M3 and M4 predict negative curvature and contain the observed *g* in their intervals, but they predict stronger relative curvature than observed (their intervals for ρ lie below `r f2(max(pi_("M3", "rho_hi"), pi_("M4", "rho_hi")))`) and a clearly negative across-cell slope, which the data do not show. Under the preregistered survival rule, which requires both the within-item curvature and the across-cell slope to fall inside a model's intervals, only M1R survived. It did so because its predictive intervals were wide enough to contain positive, zero and negative curvature.
196	
197	```{r tbl-h3}
198	#| tbl-cap: "Observed statistics compared with each model's 95% predictive interval. Survival is decided by the shape criteria (curvature and across-cell slope); level criteria are reported for completeness."
199	obs <- c(g = P$g, rho = P$rho, d = h2$slope, b = P$b, ai = w_ai)
200	t3 <- merge(pint, h3, by = "model")
201	t3 <- t3[, .(Model = model,
202	             `g [PI]` = sprintf("%s %s", ifelse(g_inside, "in", "out"), ci(g_lo, g_hi)),
203	             `ρ [PI]` = ifelse(model == "M0", "—", sprintf("%s %s", ifelse(rho_inside, "in", "out"), ci(rho_lo, rho_hi, 2))),
204	             `d [PI]` = sprintf("%s %s", ifelse(slope_inside, "in", "out"), ci(slope_lo, slope_hi)),
205	             `Survives (shape)` = ifelse(survives_shape, "yes", "no"),
206	             `b and mean index inside (level)` = ifelse(survives_level, "yes", "no"))]
207	knitr::kable(t3)
208	```
209	
210	Observed values: *g* = `r f3(obs["g"])`, ρ = `r f2(obs["rho"])`, *d* = `r f3(obs["d"])`, *b* = `r f3(obs["b"])`, weighted mean log anchoring index = `r f3(obs["ai"])`.
211	
212	## Robustness
213	
214	The within-item result held in the preregistered robustness analyses that retained the random-anchor data. Median regression without the gross-error rule gave *g* = `r f3(r_("R1_median_regression_g"))`, `r ci(r_("R1_median_regression_g", "lo"), r_("R1_median_regression_g", "hi"))`. Replacing the curvature term by separate slopes for near and far anchors showed that the slope for anchors more than one log unit from the true value differed from the slope near the true value by `r f2(r_("R2_far_minus_near_slope"))`, `r ci(r_("R2_far_minus_near_slope", "lo"), r_("R2_far_minus_near_slope", "hi"), 2)`. Without @bahnik2021 the estimate was similar but very imprecise, *g* = `r f3(r_("R3_without_bahnik_g"))`, `r ci(r_("R3_without_bahnik_g", "lo"), r_("R3_without_bahnik_g", "hi"), 2)`.
215	
216	The across-cell slope stayed positive and imprecise in most checks: with design covariates, *d* = `r f3(r_("R5_covariates_slope"))`, `r ci(r_("R5_covariates_slope", "lo"), r_("R5_covariates_slope", "hi"))`; with the largest anchor distance as the extremity measure, `r f3(r_("R7_max_distance_slope"))`, `r ci(r_("R7_max_distance_slope", "lo"), r_("R7_max_distance_slope", "hi"))`; with the log ratio of the anchors, `r f3(r_("R7_log_spread_slope"))`, `r ci(r_("R7_log_spread_slope", "lo"), r_("R7_log_spread_slope", "hi"))`. Without Weber et al. (2021), whose item coding was questioned in a later correction, the slope was `r f3(r_("R6_without_weber_slope"))`, `r ci(r_("R6_without_weber_slope", "lo"), r_("R6_without_weber_slope", "hi"))`, the only check in which the interval excluded zero. The raw-scale anchoring index, which the preregistration designated as descriptive because a constant log-scale weight does not imply a constant raw-scale index, gave `r f3(r_("R4_raw_index_slope"))`, `r ci(r_("R4_raw_index_slope", "lo"), r_("R4_raw_index_slope", "hi"))`.
217	
218	## Exploratory analyses
219	
220	The following analyses were not preregistered.
221	
222	*Both sides of the true value.* The curvature was negative both for anchors below the true value, *g* = `r f3(x_("E1_xx_neg"))`, `r ci(x_("E1_xx_neg", "lo"), x_("E1_xx_neg", "hi"))`, and for anchors above it, *g* = `r f3(x_("E1_xx_pos"))`, `r ci(x_("E1_xx_pos", "lo"), x_("E1_xx_pos", "hi"))`.
223	
224	*Item by item.* In each of the `r e2[!is.na(diff), .N]` cells with at least 20 estimates both within and beyond one log unit of the true value, the slope for far anchors was lower than the slope for near anchors (median difference `r f2(median(e2$diff, na.rm = TRUE))`).
225	
226	*Standardised effect sizes.* Across cells, Hedges' *g* rose with extremity by `r f2(x_("E3_hedges_g_slope"))` per log unit, `r ci(x_("E3_hedges_g_slope", "lo"), x_("E3_hedges_g_slope", "hi"), 2)` ([@fig-across], panel B), in line with @roseler2022meta. The same cells therefore show a rising standardised effect and no detectable change in proportional pull.
227	
228	*Extremity relative to response spread.* The across-cell extremity measure ignores how uncertain people are about each quantity. When we divided extremity by the spread of log estimates within each anchor condition (a measure that is itself affected by anchoring), the slope turned negative, *d* = `r f3(x_("E4_slope_on_scaled_extremity"))`, `r ci(x_("E4_slope_on_scaled_extremity", "lo"), x_("E4_slope_on_scaled_extremity", "hi"))`. This is consistent with original authors having placed anchors further from the truth for quantities that people know less well.
229	
230	*Relaxed calibration.* To check whether the model failures stem from the calibration to Jacowitz and Kahneman's index, we drew 300 parameter sets per model from wide ranges without calibration and simulated each on the OpAQ designs. No parameter set of any model reproduced the observed *b*, *g*, *d* and mean index jointly (all four inside their observed 95% confidence intervals). Within-item *b* and *g* together were reproduced by `r e5[model == "M4"]$within_b_and_g` of 300 M4 draws, `r e5[model == "M1R"]$within_b_and_g` M1R draws and `r e5[model == "M3"]$within_b_and_g` M3 draws, and by no M1 or M2 draw; the across-cell *d* and mean index together were reproduced by `r e5[model == "M2"]$across_d_and_ai` M2 draws and `r e5[model == "M1"]$across_d_and_ai` M1 draws, and by no M3 or M4 draw.
231	
232	## Sensitivity analyses
233	
234	These analyses were added after a code review and were not preregistered.
235	
236	*Calibration scale.* The preregistered calibration compared the models' log-scale anchoring index with Jacowitz and Kahneman's value of about .49, which they computed on the raw scale. Recalibrating every model to a raw-scale index accepted largely the same parameter values (`r paste(sprintf("%s: %d of %d", s1acc$model, s1acc$both, s1acc$log_scale), collapse = "; ")` of the originally accepted grid points were also accepted), and new predictions from the recalibrated models led to the same conclusion: only M1R survived the shape criteria.
237	
238	*Dependence on single studies (H1).* Leaving out any one of the three smaller studies left the curvature negative with confidence intervals excluding zero (*g* from `r f3(min(s_("S2_without_Frech et al., 2021"), s_("S2_without_Yoon et al., 2021, Form C"), s_("S2_without_Imhoff & Barker, 2022, Study 2")))` to `r f3(max(s_("S2_without_Frech et al., 2021"), s_("S2_without_Yoon et al., 2021, Form C"), s_("S2_without_Imhoff & Barker, 2022, Study 2")))`). Adding study-level random effects gave *g* = `r f3(s_("S2_study_random_effect"))`, `r ci(s_("S2_study_random_effect", "lo"), s_("S2_study_random_effect", "hi"))`. The single fixed-anchor item with 20 anchor levels [Imhoff and Barker, 2022, unpublished data] showed a negative curvature on its own, *g* = `r f3(s_("S2_imhoff_barker_only"))`, `r ci(s_("S2_imhoff_barker_only", "lo"), s_("S2_imhoff_barker_only", "hi"))`.
239	
240	*Influence and clustering (H2).* The across-cell slope was not robust. With study-clustered robust standard errors, *d* = `r f3(s_("S3_cluster_robust_slope"))`, `r ci(s_("S3_cluster_robust_slope", "lo"), s_("S3_cluster_robust_slope", "hi"))`. The ten most precise cells carried `r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * s_("S3_top10_weight_share"))` of the inverse-variance weight; without them, *d* = `r f3(s_("S3_without_top10_weight_cells"))`, `r ci(s_("S3_without_top10_weight_cells", "lo"), s_("S3_without_top10_weight_cells", "hi"))`. Leaving out one study at a time gave slopes between `r f3(s_("S3_loo_slope_range", "lo"))` and `r f3(s_("S3_loo_slope_range", "hi"))`.
241	
242	# Discussion
243	
244	Within items, anchors lost proportional pull as they moved away from the true value. Near the truth, the local elasticity was `r f2(P$b)`; for anchors a factor of 2.7 from the truth it was `r f2(loc_el(1))`, and for anchors a factor of 7.4 away, `r f2(loc_el(2))`. The decline appeared on both sides of the true value, in every item with enough near and far anchors, and in the one fixed-anchor item with many anchor levels. Across two-anchor studies, where authors chose one anchor pair per item, the anchoring index showed no detectable decline, and its point estimate leaned the other way.
245	
246	## What the within-item result rules out
247	
248	The negative curvature contradicts two simple accounts. Anchor-and-adjust with a fixed number of steps predicts that far anchors keep more of their distance, because a bounded number of bounded steps cannot correct a large gap; the data show the reverse. Constant-weight integration, the simplest version of the anchor integration model, predicts no change in proportional pull; it too is contradicted. The accounts that predict a decline share one feature: the anchor's influence is limited by how plausible it is. This holds for adjustment that stops at the edge of the plausible range [@epley2006], for integration that discounts implausible anchors [@wegener2001; @turner2016], and for a resource-rational agent who invests more adjustments when the anchor is far off [@lieder2018a]. The result fits earlier experiments with few anchor levels in which implausible anchors had proportionally smaller effects [@chapman1994; @mussweiler2001; @wegener2001] and the distance-decaying anchoring weight of @barrera2024, now shown with open-ended quantities and anchors varied within items.
249	
250	The decline was smaller than M3 and M4 predicted. Their relative curvature intervals lay below the observed value, which means that far anchors still pulled estimates more than a hard plausibility boundary or a steep plausibility discount allows. A mixture in which the weight of an anchor falls gradually but does not vanish could describe this. The data do not identify such a model, and we did not test one.
251	
252	## The across-cell pattern
253	
254	The across-cell analysis did not reproduce the within-item decline, and no model with a single parameter set reproduced both patterns. Two explanations are plausible, and our data cannot fully separate them. First, extremity measured against the true value is not extremity measured against people's uncertainty. Researchers may place anchors further from the truth for quantities that people know poorly. An anchor ten times the true population of a city may be less implausible than an anchor twice the height of a familiar building. When we scaled extremity by the spread of estimates, the across-cell slope turned negative, as the within-item analysis and the plausibility accounts predict. Because that spread is itself affected by anchoring, this analysis is suggestive only. Second, the two sets differ in anchor type: the within-item set is mostly random anchors, and the across-cell set only fixed or relevant anchors. The models make the same shape predictions for both, but it is possible that informative anchors lose less pull with extremity than anchors people know to be random. The fixed-anchor stratum of the within-item set pointed in the same direction as the random-anchor stratum but was too small for the preregistered test, and only one fixed-anchor item had enough anchor levels to show the decline on its own.
255	
256	The divergence also bears on how moderator analyses of anchoring should be read. In the same cells, the standardised effect rose with extremity while the proportional index did not change detectably. Meta-analytic findings that larger anchor distances produce larger standardised effects [@roseler2022meta] therefore say little about whether extreme anchors are more influential per unit of distance. Tests of anchoring theories need a proportional outcome and variation in extremity that the researcher controls.
257	
258	## Limitations
259	
260	The primary evidence rests largely on one study. Thirteen of the 20 within-item cells, and `r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * 6578 / dc$within_rows)` of the within-item estimates, come from @bahnik2021, in which participants compared 13 random anchors with 13 different lengths and heights. Without this study the within-item curvature had the same sign but a confidence interval too wide to be informative. The random anchors also differ from the fixed anchors that dominate applied settings. The preregistered test of the fixed-anchor stratum was not informative; in an exploratory analysis, the one fixed-anchor item with 20 anchor levels showed the same decline, but it is a single item. A direct test of the extremity function for informative anchors needs experiments that present many anchor levels for many items.
261	
262	Second, extremity was measured relative to the true value, not relative to each participant's belief. Where people systematically over- or underestimate a quantity, the anchor's distance from their belief differs from its distance from the truth. The simulations included item-level bias to account for this, and the curvature was negative on both sides of the true value. However, a study that elicits unanchored estimates or plausible ranges from the same participants would give a cleaner measure.
263	
264	Third, the models were specified on the log scale and calibrated to a single external benchmark. The shape predictions of M1, M2, M3 and M4 follow from their structure and held across all calibrated parameter values, but the level predictions depend on the calibration, and the resource-rational model's predictions depend strongly on its time cost and on how uncertain people are. That this model survived our tests reflects the width of its predictions more than a close fit. Formal tests of resource-rational anchoring need independent measures of the time cost and of people's uncertainty.
265	
266	Fourth, OpAQ harmonises data from many studies, and harmonisation can introduce errors. We found one item whose responses were recorded in different units from its anchors and true value, and a later correction questioned the item coding of another study. Our rules removed the first; excluding the second made the across-cell slope positive and significant. We used only positive ratio-scale quantities with open response scales, so the results do not speak to dates, percentages, bounded scales or preferences.
267	
268	## Conclusion
269	
270	Within the same questions, extreme anchors pulled estimates by a smaller share of their distance than moderate anchors. This contradicts anchor-and-adjust with a fixed number of steps and constant-weight integration, and supports accounts in which an anchor's influence is limited by its plausibility, although the decline was weaker than simple plausibility models predict. Across studies with researcher-chosen anchors, the pattern was not visible, which suggests that comparisons across items confound anchor extremity with how well people know the quantity. For anyone choosing an anchor, the within-item evidence implies diminishing returns to extremity. For researchers, it implies that the extremity function should be estimated within items and with proportional measures.
271	
272	# Declarations
273	
274	**Data, code and materials.** The OpAQ data are openly available under CC-BY 4.0 at https://osf.io/ygnvb [@opaqosf]. All code, the preregistration, the frozen predictions, all outputs and the review records are available in the project repository [repository link to be added before submission]. `run_all.sh` reproduces all results from the raw data.
275	
276	**Preregistration.** The preregistration is `prereg/preregistration.md` in the repository, committed before any estimate was read (git tag `prereg-v1`, 27 September 2026). Deviations are listed in `deviations.md` and summarised above.
277	
278	**Use of artificial intelligence.** This study was conceived, designed, coded, analysed and written by an AI system, Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), working autonomously in the Claude Code environment between 27 and 28 September 2026 under the instruction of the author, who set the task (a complete, preregistered study in judgement and decision making using open data) and its constraints. The AI chose the research question, dataset, models and analyses, wrote all code and text, and recorded its decisions in `decision_log.md`. Two other AI systems reviewed the design, code and manuscript: OpenAI Codex CLI and Google Gemini 3.8 Flash (via the Antigravity CLI); their comments and the responses are in `review_log.md`. All references were retrieved from Crossref or DataCite metadata by script. The author is accountable for the content of the article. No AI system is listed as an author.
279	
280	**Ethics.** The study used only openly licensed, anonymised secondary data; no new data were collected, and no ethics approval was sought.
281

# Novelty check: anchoring vs anchor extremity (classic papers) - working notes

## Strack & Mussweiler 1997 JPSP 73:437-446, doi 10.1037/0022-3514.73.3.437 (verified Crossref)
- Study 3 (n=67, within-subject, 8 items, Latin square): plausible anchors ~1 SD from calibration mean (n=151), implausible >10 SD. Table 5 p.442 anchors; Table 6 p.443 z-values: plausible H .04 / L -.13 (diff .17); implausible H .25 / L -.17 (diff .42). Interaction F(1,66)=3.55 p<.07. Appendix p.446 per-item raw means (several rows implausible: Einstein, Gandhi, Da Vinci reversed).

## Mussweiler & Strack 2001 Soc Cog 19:145-160, doi 10.1521/soco.19.2.145.20705 (verified)
- Study 1 Antarctic mean temp (true -68): anchors -43, -17 (plausible, ~1SD), 700, 900 (implausible, 56 & 72 SD). Table 1 p.154: -41.12, -24.84, -23.27, -24.44. n 15-16/cell.
- Study 2 Gandhi age (true 78): anchors 61, 86 (+-1SD), 214, 271 (18, 26 SD). Table 2 p.156: 62.92, 70.36, 75.26, 72.86. n 26-28/cell.

## Wegener, Petty, Detweiler-Bedell & Jarvis 2001 JESP 37:62-69, doi 10.1006/jesp.2000.1431 (verified)
- 8 items, within-subject 2x2; z-standardized estimates. Exp1A (n=151) moderate H/L +.50/-.52 vs extreme +.37/-.36; Exp1B (n=145) moderate +.52/-.41 vs very extreme +.15/-.25; Exp2 (n=80, no 'random' instruction) moderate +.40/-.47 vs very extreme +.26/-.19 (p.65-66). Plausibility ratings 1.28 vs 4.38 (9-pt). Appendix p.68 anchors (6 levels per item).

## Wegener, Petty, Blankenship & Detweiler-Bedell 2010 JCP 20:5-16, doi 10.1016/j.jcps.2009.12.003 (verified)
- No new numbers. Footnote 1 p.7 and p.12: cites Wegener, Blankenship, Detweiler-Bedell & Petty (2009) raw data 'Knowledge and anchor extremity': smaller effects with low- and high-extremity than moderate; downturn earlier for high-knowledge.

## Bystranowski et al. 2021 LHB 45:1-23, doi 10.1037/lhb0000438 (verified)
- Table 4 p.12 (control vs anchor): low k=4 d=.43; medium k=42 d=.59; high k=5 d=.19; continuous coef -.04 (z), -.08 (d). Table 5 p.13 (high vs low): low k=5 d=.82; medium k=25 d=1.00; high k=7 d=.77. Anchor value = z of anchor magnitude between studies, binned at 25th/75th pct.

## Schultze et al. 2015 JDM 10:144-171, doi 10.1017/s1930297500003922 (verified)
- Advice distance 5-75% (Exp1), up to 150% (Exp3). AT = -0.093 -0.003 d + 0.153 ln d (Table 1 p.151). Pooled 6 exps p.166-167: B1=-0.002, B2=0.101, peak at 63.84%. Absolute shift ~ proportional to distance (SRM), no decrease at far distances.

## Harris et al. 2019 JEP:G, doi 10.1037/xge0000644 (accepted MS)
- Table 2 p.23; anchors p.17 (8/20 C; 6000/30000 GBP) and p.27 (2/25 C; 13000/200000 GBP).

## Simmons, LeBoeuf & Nelson 2010 JPSP 99:917-932, doi 10.1037/a0021540 (Penn repository MS)
- Study 3a/3b single-anchor plausible vs implausible (Tables 2-3, MS p.47-48). Note 2 (MS p.42): implausible anchors produced larger anchoring (estimates further from truth) for 6/8 items. No means per level.

## Lieder et al. 2018 PBR 25:322-349, doi 10.3758/s13423-017-1286-8 (preprint version)
- Eq 3-4: E[x^] = a r^t + (1-r^t) x -> constant relative adjustment. Fig 10 (MS p.21): R&S 1989 Attila data approx 630/680/790/885/990 for anchors 500..1300 (read off figure; SECONDARY); model slope ~0.95; MTurk replication approx 590/645/870/970/1020. J&K AI empirical mean 48.48% over 15 items (MS p.17) SECONDARY.

## Frederick & Mochon 2012 JEP:G 141:124-133, doi 10.1037/a0024006 - no extremity manipulation.

## Additional (second pass)
- Chapman & Johnson 1994 JBDM 7:223-242, doi 10.1002/bdm.3960070402 (verified). Full text NOT obtained; figures (Exhibits 1-4, 6) from author's academia.edu upload. Exp1 anchors 0.1/0.7/1.3/1.9 x EV (Exhibit 2); Exhibit 3 p.229 geo-mean prices ~74/106.5/127/127.5; Exhibit 4 p.230 by lottery range (very narrow ~84/104/122/111 inverted-U). Exp2 Exhibit 6 p.234 monetary anchors 1.08-28.16 x EV: ~182/248/297/344 (level multipliers unknown).
- Turner & Schley 2016 Cog Psych 90:1-47 doi 10.1016/j.cogpsych.2016.07.003 (lab-site PDF). Sec 5.3.2 p.23-24: mapping function assumes inverted-U (from Wegener 2001), kmax allows asymptote; Fig 9. Exps use single anchor per item.
- Smith, Windschitl & Bruchmann 2013 EJSP 43:97-108 doi 10.1002/ejsp.1921: hypothesised plateau (Fig 3, p.105), not tested.
- Hardt & Pohl 2003 Memory 11:379-394 doi 10.1080/09658210244000504: abstract only (PubMed); Fig 4 reproduced in Wilson, Arora, Zhang & Griffiths (CogSci paper, cocosci.princeton.edu/papers/wilson_rational.pdf) Fig 1.
- Townson 2019 MSU dissertation doi 10.25335/p9dm-7a29 (DataCite verified): abstract 'Extremity of the anchor was found to slightly weaken the impact'; k=84 r effect sizes.
- Marti & Wissler 2000 JEP:Applied 6:91-103 doi 10.1037/1076-898x.6.2.91: abstract: award rises with request but decreases with most extreme request.
- Thorsteinson 2011 JASP 41:1774-1792 doi 10.1111/j.1559-1816.2011.00779.x: abstract only.
- Lee, Lee & Kim 2022 Korean J Cog Sci 33(1):77-93 doi 10.19066/cogsci.2022.33.1.004 (resolves to KCI; not in Crossref): abstract only.
- Computed AIs: see scratch_nov_classic_ai.py / _ai_out.txt
- Northcraft & Neale 1987 OBHDP 39:84-97 doi 10.1016/0749-5978(87)90046-x: full text; 4 anchors; AIs in _ai_out.txt

Base directory for this skill: ~/.claude/skills/download-paper

# Download & Verify Academic Papers

`$SKILL_DIR` below is wherever this skill lives (e.g. `~/.claude/skills/download-paper`).

## Step 1: Try downloading the PDF

```bash
PDF_PATH=$($SKILL_DIR/download_paper.py --doi "DOI_HERE" 2>/tmp/download_paper.log)
```

Run the script directly — its shebang is `uv run --script`, which installs
[`fetchpdf`](https://github.com/The-Metascience-Observatory/fetchpdf) into a managed
environment on first use (a few seconds); later runs reuse uv's cache. The fetchpdf version
is pinned to a commit hash in the script's `# dependencies` header; edit that hash to update.

Sources, in order:

1. Cache (a copy of this DOI fetched earlier)
2. The fetchpdf open-access chain: OpenAlex, Unpaywall, PubMed Central, Europe PMC,
   Crossref links, Semantic Scholar, arXiv and other preprint servers, repository
   landing pages, publisher routes
3. Google Scholar via SerpAPI
4. The user's running, signed-in Chrome — one throwaway tab walks the Scholar links plain
   HTTP could not fetch, then the publisher's own PDF URLs (canonical URL by DOI prefix,
   `citation_pdf_url` from the landing page, ScienceDirect `/pdfft`), then EBSCOhost

Every downloaded PDF is checked against the requested DOI, title and page range. A
different paper, or a publisher preview of only the first page, is discarded and the walk
moves on to the next candidate.

**What the Chrome step needs** (it logs one line and skips when any of these is missing):

- macOS, with Google Chrome already running and at least one window open
- Chrome signed in to the publisher or EBSCO through the user's institution / OpenAthens
- *View ▸ Developer ▸ Allow JavaScript from Apple Events* switched on once
- `INSTITUTION_EBSCO_PROFILE` set to the library's EBSCO cluster id, for the EBSCO candidate

The step opens its tab at the end of the front window, never focuses it, and closes it
again on the way out, so it does not disturb what the user is doing.

Options:

- `--title "Paper Title"` — the Google Scholar query; otherwise taken from Crossref
- `--force` — re-download even if cached
- `--no-browser` — skip the Chrome step (leaves the run entirely non-interactive)
- `--playwright` — let fetchpdf render JS-heavy pages in a headless browser. Slower, and
  Cloudflare-protected publishers block it, so it is off by default.
- `--open` — on failure, open the best candidate URL in the user's browser for manual download

Exit codes: 0 = success (path on stdout), 1 = failure, 2 = opened in browser for manual download.

## Step 2: Read the downloaded PDF

```bash
pdftotext "$PDF_PATH" - | head -200           # First 200 lines
pdftotext "$PDF_PATH" - | grep -A5 "keyword"  # Search for specific claims
```

## Step 3: When the download fails

The script lists its candidate URLs on stderr, each with a note:

1. `[Scholar link, no PDF by plain HTTP]` — a PDF link Google Scholar offered that returned
   403, a bot check, or a landing page. The Chrome step tries these first when it runs.
2. `[Scholar link, a different paper]` — fetched, but not this DOI's paper. Skip it.
3. `[publisher page]` — `https://doi.org/DOI_HERE`, which honours institutional access

Three manual routes, in the order worth trying.

### 3a: Sign in at this publisher, then re-run

One OpenAthens handshake covers one publisher. A login at publisher A does not
authenticate publisher B, and the Chrome step can only use sessions that already exist.
Ask the user to open the `[publisher page]` URL, click *Access through your institution*,
and say when they are through; then re-run Step 1 with `--force`.

### 3b: Read the paper off the page

When no PDF exists to download (a landing page with the full text in HTML, an
Academia.edu or ResearchGate record), read the content instead. `browser-use --browser
real` drives the user's Chrome and returns structured page content — abstract, key
findings, figure captions, references — which is often enough for claim verification.

```bash
uvx browser-use --browser real open "PAPER_URL"
uvx browser-use state          # structured page content; repeat after `scroll down`
uvx browser-use close          # always close when done
```

`browser-use` is unreliable against heavy JS apps such as the EBSCO viewer: `state` and
`eval` come back empty there. Use it for ordinary publisher pages.

### 3c: Run one route on its own

`institutional_fetch.py` holds the Chrome layer Step 1 uses, and its CLI runs a single
route against one DOI — useful for debugging a route or for the cookie-jar route, which
Step 1 does not use.

```bash
$SKILL_DIR/institutional_fetch.py --doi "10.1037/edu0000827" --ebsco 2>/tmp/inst.log
$SKILL_DIR/institutional_fetch.py --doi "..." --ebsco --all-db   # beyond PsycInfo
$SKILL_DIR/institutional_fetch.py export-cookies                 # once, after logging in
$SKILL_DIR/institutional_fetch.py --doi "10.1080/..." 2>/tmp/inst.log   # cookie-jar route
```

Success prints the verified PDF's path on stdout (same contract as `download_paper.py`).

### Critical gotchas (learned the hard way)

- **Verify page 1 against the DOI or title for anything you fetch by hand.** Title-based
  search returns topically-similar papers under the DOI you asked for, and a mislabelled
  PDF silently corrupts whatever dataset it lands in. `download_paper.py` and
  `institutional_fetch.py` both run fetchpdf's identity check themselves; the `browser-use`
  route does not.
- **Navigate before you fetch.** Cross-origin fetch of a publisher PDF is CORS-blocked. The
  Chrome step navigates the tab to the PDF URL first, waits until
  `document.contentType == 'application/pdf'`, then fetches same-origin with credentials —
  the asset host (`pdf.sciencedirectassets.com`, silverchair, `content.ebscohost.com`) is
  same-origin once the tab is on it. The wait also lets Cloudflare, Anubis and Imperva
  interstitials clear themselves, which they do in a real browser and never under curl.
- **Chrome's PDF viewer cannot return a Promise to AppleScript.** The in-page fetch parks
  its base64 on `window.__pdf`; a poll collects it and reads it back in 800k-character
  chunks. A plain `return await fetch(...)` yields an empty string with no error.
- **Chrome's AppleScript tab `id` compares as a string.** `if (id of tt as string) is "…"`
  matches; a numeric `=` matches nothing and every command silently does nothing.
- **`Content-Disposition: attachment` URLs never reach the viewer.** Chrome drops the file
  in `~/Downloads` and the tab stays put, so the wait times out. Prefer the inline PDF URL
  of a pair (`/doi/pdf/…` over `/doi/pdfdirect/…?download=true`).
- **Signed EBSCO content URLs need no cookies.** `content.ebscohost.com/cds/retrieve?content=<token>`
  authenticates itself; plain `curl` downloads it. Don't rebuild the cookie dance for it.
- **EBSCO failure modes are informative.** No record id means EBSCO does not index the
  paper; a record with no content URL means EBSCO has "Linked Full Text" only — a link-out
  to the publisher, not a hosted PDF.
- **Domain-aware cookies.** A real browser holds thousands of cookies. Sending all of them to
  one host returns **`400 Request Header Or Cookie Too Large`**. The cookie-jar route builds
  a per-domain `RequestsCookieJar` so requests sends only the target host's cookies.
- **Off-campus IP gating is real.** Even in a logged-in real Chrome, SAGE / Wiley / T&F / OUP
  / IOS / Springer / BMJ direct routes are frequently campus-IP-gated. EBSCO is not. Keep a
  VPN / on-campus batch list rather than retrying.
- **Expect a low yield on paywalled batches.** One real batch: 62 paywalled papers → 8
  fetched. Plan around partial coverage.
- **The EBSCO viewer changes.** If the resource-timings lookup stops finding a
  `cds/retrieve` URL, check the viewer's network tab and the
  `research.ebsco.com/api/researcher-edge-aggregator/v1/records/<id>/fulltext/pdf?...&intent=download`
  JSON endpoint before rebuilding the flow.

## Environment Variables

Keys are read from the environment, then from `~/.claude/api_keys.env`.

- `SERPAPI_API_KEYS` (comma-separated) or `SERPAPI_API_KEY` — enables the Google Scholar
  step. Keys are tried in order; an exhausted or invalid key moves on to the next.
- `INSTITUTION_EBSCO_PROFILE` — the library's EBSCO cluster id, the `<cluster>` in the
  `research.ebsco.com/c/<cluster>/...` URL Chrome lands on after an institutional login.
  Enables the EBSCO candidate in the Chrome step.
- `CORE_API_KEY`, `ELSEVIER_API_KEY`, `OPENALEX_API_KEY` — optional; passed to fetchpdf's
  CORE, Elsevier text-mining and OpenAlex sources.
- `RESEARCHER_EMAIL` or `EMAIL` — contact address for the open-access APIs (Unpaywall
  requires one; Crossref gives a higher rate limit with one).

## Cache

Downloaded PDFs are cached in `~/.claude/cache/pdfs/` (MD5 of DOI). Use `--force` to re-download.

experiments. Therefore, we believe that anchoring effects are larger in the laboratory.

Anchor Extremeness

       Another area where anchoring theories have diverged to some extent involves the

question of whether more extreme anchors lead to larger anchoring effects. For example, a

researcher can choose a question for which the true value is 42 and use an anchor that is not

extreme, such as 50, but also an extreme anchor, such as 500. According to the Insufficient

Adjustment Model, people adjust until they arrive at their range of plausible values (Epley &

Gilovich, 2004). For example, if plausible values for the length of a sentence range from 2 to 30

words for a person, it should not matter whether the anchor is 50 or 500, but it should matter

whether it is 20 or 50. In the former case, the estimate would be 30 regardless of the anchor, but

in the latter case, the person would not adjust the 20 but would rather use it as an estimate. As
 ANCHORING EFFECTS META-ANALYSIS                                                             11



people’s personal ranges of plausible values are unknown in almost all paradigms, no clear

prediction can be derived from the Insufficient Adjustment Model.

       A clear hypothesis can be derived from the Selective Accessibility Model: Extreme

primes can be excluded from the judgment-forming process and thus lead to contrast effects

(e.g., Mussweiler, 2002; Schwarz & Bless, 1992). That is, an anchor that does not seem to have

much to do with a plausible estimate might highlight dissimilarities and make the target stimulus

appear less like the anchor (see also Sherif et al., 1958). Previous studies have found nonlinear

relationships between anchor extremeness and anchoring effect size (Chapman & Johnson, 1994;

Thorsteinson, 2011), but there is also evidence that this relationship might be an inverted u-shape

(Bystranowski et al., 2021, p. 13; Townson, 2019). Notably, paradigms that measure adjustment

steps and adjustment step sizes have shown that even adjustment is nonlinear such that initial

large adjustments are followed by more fine-grained adjustments (Frech et al., 2020; Röseler,

Schütz, Dolling, et al., 2020).

       As most anchoring questions assess only two anchors, and each participant is presented

with only one of them (one is larger and one is smaller than the correct answer), we

operationalized anchor extremeness that was based on the true value as the mean relative

anchoring distance from the true value per anchoring item. That is, we computed the mean of the

absolute distance between the anchor and the true value (in cases where a true value existed)

divided by the true value such that a value of 1 indicated that the anchors were equal to the true

values and a value of 2 meant that anchors were on average 2 (or 1/2) times the true value.

Description of Stimuli

       For anchoring effects, a property of a stimulus (e.g., height of the Eiffel tower) has to be

estimated. In most studies, researchers simply ask participants whether the Eiffel tower is taller
 ANCHORING EFFECTS META-ANALYSIS                                                             12



---
other than the Random-Effects Multilevel Model, data had to be aggregated by study.

Moderator Analyses

       We conducted independent tests of moderators using multilevel random-effects models

and significance tests (Viechtbauer, 2010). Among continuous moderators (Table 2), only the

anchor distance had an effect on the anchoring effect size, which was positive. Among

categorical moderators (Table 3), type of anchor (no effects for subliminal or random anchors

and large effects for fixed and relevant anchors), type of task (e.g., largest effect for predicted

happiness, no effect for price estimates), comparative questions (small effect for paradigms

without comparative questions, large effect for those with comparative questions), and type of

stimulus (no effect for audio/visual/image, large effect for brief written descriptions) affected

anchoring effect size.

next explain how our findings (see Table 4) are related to previous research.

Moderators of Anchoring Effects

       The relative distance between anchors and true values was strongly associated with the

size of anchoring effects, with more extreme anchors leading to larger effect sizes. The

proportion of female participants, the sample mean age, the publication year, and monetary

incentives for participation or for accuracy did not affect anchoring effect size. Note that

incentives for accurate estimation not reducing anchoring is only partly consistent with past

---

Findings Regarding Theories on Anchoring

       Our results bring clarity to the controversies that existing anchoring theories have been

facing: The Insufficient Adjustment Model was not supported in that incentives did not decrease

anchoring. The Selective Accessibility Model’s prediction that extreme anchors can lead to

smaller (or even negative) effects was not supported. Instead, anchoring extremeness was related

in a nonlinear but positive way to anchoring effect size. Finally, none of our findings

contradicted any of the two predictions derived on the basis of the Scale Distortion Theory. Note,

however, that the theory is already facing contradictory evidence with respect to variables not
---



certain river. Note that target stimuli (e.g., points in a scatterplot) are superior to everyday

knowledge questions in that they are scalable. Participants can even receive two stimuli with the

same true value (e.g., 42 dots) and different anchors (e.g., 21 and 84) without even noticing that

they have already seen the stimulus.

        We believe that future research would benefit from exploring more precise measures than

effect sizes such as Cohen’s d or Hedges’s g. For example, the relative strength of adjustment

could be used because it provides a unitless and general metric. Standardized measures could

help to formalize the relationship between anchor distance and adjustment strength as has been

done in similar fields (e.g., Schultze et al., 2015).

Anchoring Research as a Poster Child for Open Science

        As we found almost as many preregistered studies (k = 182) as nonpreregistered studies

(k = 211), we are optimistic that the field of anchoring is adopting new standards of open
---
by the Selective Accessibility Model and Scale Distortion Theory but not by the Insufficient

Adjustment Model.

       In reviewing recent findings from studies that evaluated anchoring theories, we identified

only two domains in which theories made different predictions, first, that time pressure leads to

stronger anchoring effects according to the Insufficient Adjustment Model (Epley & Gilovich,

2006, pp. 312-313) but smaller anchoring effects according to the Selective Accessibility Model

(Englich & Soder, 2009). Previous findings either supported the Insufficient Adjustment Model

(Lieder et al., 2018b; Yik et al., 2019) or spoke against both accounts (Chaxel, 2014). Second,

anchoring extremeness is related to anchoring effects in a positive way, according to the

Insufficient Adjustment Model, but based on the Selective Accessibility Model, anchors that are

too high or too low should lead to smaller anchoring effects (i.e., an inverted u-shaped

relationship between anchor extremeness and anchoring effect size).

       Apart from theories contradicting each other, there are findings that contradict predictions
yet been a systematic analysis of the relationships between paradigm features and effect sizes.

Contradictory Findings

       Moreover, many moderator effects have been reported in only a single study or have

subsequently encountered contradictory findings. For example, there are contradictory reports on

the relationship between anchor extremeness and effect size: Chapman and Johnson (1994)

reported a nonlinear relationship, but they used the geometric (instead of the more widely used

arithmetic) mean of estimates, but using the geometric mean would result in a nonlinear

relationship for extreme anchors even if anchoring effects increased in a linear fashion.

Thorsteinson (2011) found nonlinearity, but it was confounded with plausibility. Finally, meta-

analyses (Bystranowski et al., 2021; Townson, 2019) have suggested that there may even be an

inverted u-shaped relationship.

       The question of whether extremely high anchors produce effects is crucial in practical

settings. For example, if you are negotiating over the price of a book and make the first offer,

you will want to know whether your offer is outrageously high or not. However, the exact

relationship between anchor extremeness and anchoring effect size is still not clear. Similarly,

SUSCEPTILITY TO ANCHORING EFFECTS




                        Testing the Reliability of Anchoring Susceptibility Scores

                                      Lucia Weber1 and Lukas Röseler2




       1
           Faculty of Medicine, University of Zurich, Switzerland

       2
           Münster Center for Open Science, University of Münster, Germany




                                                Author Note

       Lucia Weber

       Lukas Röseler       https://orcid.org/0000-0002-6446-1901

       Correspondence concerning this article should be addressed to Lukas Röseler, University

of Münster. Email: [email redacted]




                                             Preprint Version

       This manuscript corresponds to the corrected version of the article published in EJOP

(February 2025). This manuscript has not been peer reviewed in this form.
 SUSCEPTIBILITY TO ANCHORING EFFECTS


                                                Abstract

Whereas anchoring is a very robust and well-known effect that refers to the assimilation of

numeric estimates toward previously considered numbers, the psychological mechanisms

behind it have yet to be fully clarified. Research on theories on how susceptibility to

anchoring is related to other personality parameters has not been able to provide sufficient

empirical evidence of such relationships. A probable explanation is that anchoring scores lack

reliability in most anchoring experiments. The present research examined whether reliability

depends on the type of score used to capture anchoring susceptibility. In a classical anchoring

experiment, men and women aged between 14 and 67 years (N = 78) were asked to estimate

the true values of certain numbers (e.g., height of the Zugspitze mountain) after being

confronted with either a high or a low anchor number. Four different anchoring scores that are

commonly used to measure susceptibility to anchoring in anchoring research were computed

for every person, as well as the scores’ reliabilities. The number and types of items were

chosen to allow for reliable and valid measurement. Anchoring effects were present, but the

reliabilities of all four scores were either very low or zero. These results reinforce the

reliability problem that was also described by previous research. So far, there are no

conditions under which anchoring susceptibility can be measured reliably, suggesting the

development of new measures or even questioning the existence of individual differences in

susceptibility to anchoring. In further research, other person-independent factors that may

influence anchoring strength should be investigated to develop theories that can explain the

psychological mechanisms behind anchoring.

Keywords: anchoring, anchoring effect, anchoring scores, anchoring strength, reliability
 SUSCEPTIBILITY TO ANCHORING EFFECTS

Anchoring describes the phenomenon that people are influenced by a previously considered

number when making a numerical estimate. In studies on the anchoring effect, people are

initially confronted with an anchor number—often by having to respond to a comparative

question, such as “Is the height of Mount Everest larger or smaller than 5,000 meters?” After

answering this first question, when asked to give an actual estimate, people tend to assimilate

their answer toward the anchor.

         It has been proposed that people differ in the extent to which they are susceptible to

this effect, depending on certain individual differences, such as general knowledge, cognitive

abilities (e.g., Bergman et al., 2010), or the Big Five (e.g., McElroy & Dowd, 2007). The

implicit assumption that susceptibility to anchoring is a person parameter can be found at the

core of anchoring models, which aim to clarify which psychological mechanisms underlie

anchoring effects, for example, in the Insufficient Adjustment Model (Epley & Gilovich,

2001).

                                                    Dan R. Schley
                           Rotterdam School of Management, Erasmus University, [email redacted]

                      Marshall School of Business, University of Southern California, [email redacted]


     One of the most robust phenomena studied across the social behavioral sciences is numeric anchoring, in

     which a comparison against a presumed-to-be arbitrary number preceding a judgment can influence a myriad

     of real-world-relevant judgments. The authors meta-analyze the expansive literature containing 2,601 total

     effect sizes (1,280 comparing high anchors against low anchors), finding a large (Hedges’g = 0.825, 95% CI

     [0.765, 0.884], I 2 = 93.73%) effect that remains large even after accounting for extensive publication bias. Evi-

     dence suggests reduced (or null) effects associated with incidental anchoring (i.e., numeric priming), anchors

     from different dimensions, or from random numbers, the presence of incentives or debiasing interventions,

     and whether the anchor provides directional information. The authors provide a comprehensive review of

     both the empirical and theoretical landscape, and offer recommendations for consolidating the literature,

     improving theory testing, future development of theory and methods related to anchoring, and guidance for

     managers attempting to use anchoring effects in strategic and policy decisions.

Promoting erroneous divergent opinions increases the wisdom of crowds
Federico Barrera Lermarchand1,2,3, Pablo Balenzuela2,3, Bahador Bahrami4,5,6, Ophelia Deroy7,8,9, &
Joaquin Navajas1,2,10

1 Laboratorio de Neurociencia, Universidad Torcuato Di Tella, Buenos Aires, Argentina
2 National Scientific and Technical Research Council (CONICET), Buenos Aires, Argentina
3 Departamento de Física, Facultad de Ciencias Exactas y Naturales, Universidad de Buenos Aires,
Argentina
4 Crowd Cognition Group, Department of General Psychology and Education, Ludwig Maximilian
University, Munich, Germany
5 Department of Psychology, Royal Holloway University of London, UK
6 Centre for Adaptive Rationality, Max Planck Institute for Human Development, Berlin, Germany
7 Munich Centre for Neuroscience, Ludwig Maximilian University, Munich, Germany
8 Institute of Philosophy, School of Advanced Study, University of London, London, UK
9 Faculty of Philosophy, Ludwig Maximilian University, Munich, Germany
10 Escuela de Negocios, Universidad Torcuato Di Tella, Buenos Aires, Argentina

Corresponding author: Joaquin Navajas ([email redacted])

1

 Abstract
The aggregation of many lay judgements generates surprisingly accurate estimates. This phenomenon,
called the “wisdom of crowds”, has been demonstrated in domains such as medical decision making and
financial forecasting. Previous research identified two factors driving this effect: the accuracy of
individual assessments and the diversity of opinions. Most available strategies to enhance the wisdom of
crowds have focused on improving individual accuracy while neglecting the potential of increasing
opinion diversity. Here, we study a complementary approach to reduce collective error by promoting
erroneous divergent opinions. This strategy proposes to anchor half of the crowd to a small value and the
other half to a large value before eliciting and averaging all estimates. Consistent with our mathematical
modeling, four experiments (N=1362 adults) demonstrate that this method is effective for estimation and
forecasting tasks. Beyond practical implications, these findings offer new theoretical insights into the
epistemic value of collective decision making.
Keywords: wisdom of crowds, collective intelligence, diversity, anchoring, extremization

their size and consequently the magnitude of the anchoring bias. For instance, the
anchoring bias is larger the more uncertain people are about the quantity to be
estimated (Jacowitz & Kahneman, 1995). Indeed, Wilson et al. (1996) found that
people knowledgeable about the quantity to be estimated were immune to the anchoring
bias whereas less knowledgeable people were susceptible to it. While familiarity (Wright
& Anderson, 1989) and expertise (Northcraft & Neale, 1987) do not abolish anchoring,
expertise appears to at least reduce it (Northcraft & Neale, 1987). Other experiments
have systematically varied the distance from the anchor to the correct value. Their
results suggested that the magnitude of the anchoring bias initially increases with the
distance from the anchor to the correct value (Russo & Schoemaker, 1989). Yet this
linear increase of the anchoring bias does not continue indefinitely. Chapman and
Johnson (1994) found that increasing an already unrealistically large anchor increases
the anchoring bias less than increasing a realistic anchor by the same amount.


       Critically for the resource-rational account proposed here, the computational
resources available to people also seem to influence their answers. Time pressure,
cognitive load, and alcohol decrease the size of people’s adjustments and
inter-individual differences in how much people adjust their initial estimate correlate
with relevant personality traits such as the need for cognition (Epley & Gilovich, 2006).
In addition to effects related to cognitive resources, adjustment also depends on
incentives. Intuitively, accuracy motivation should increase the size of people’s
adjustments and therefore decrease the anchoring bias. Interestingly, experiments have
found that accuracy motivation decreases the anchoring bias only in some cases, but not
two basic operations: The first operation takes in the current estimate and
stochastically modifies it to generate a new one. The second operation compares the
posterior probability of the new estimate to that of the old one and accepts or rejects
the modification stochastically. Furthermore, we assume that the cost of computation is
proportional to how many such operations have been performed. These two basic
operations are sufficient to execute an effective MCMC strategy for probabilistic
inference known as the Metropolis-Hastings algorithm (Hastings, 1970). This algorithm
is the basis for our anchoring-and-adjustment models as illustrated in Figure 1.

       To be concrete, given an initial guess x̂0 , which we will assume to be the anchor
a (x̂0 = a), this algorithm performs a series of adjustments. In each step a potential
adjustment δ is proposed by sampling from a symmetric probability distribution Pprop
(δ ∼ Pprop , Pprop (−δ) = Pprop (δ)). The adjustment will either be accepted, that is
x̂t+1 = x̂t + δ, or rejected, that is xt+1 = x̂t . If a proposed adjustment makes the
estimate more probable (P (X = x̂t + δ|K) > P (X = x̂t |K)), then it will always be
accepted. Otherwise the adjustment will be made with probability α = PP(X=x̂ t +δ|K)
                                                                        (X=x̂t |K)
                                                                                     ,
that is according to the posterior probability of the adjusted relative to the unadjusted
estimate. This strategy ensures that regardless of which initial value you start from, the
frequency with which each value x has been considered will eventually equal to its
subjective probability of being correct, that is P (X = x|K). This is necessary to
capture the finding that the distribution of people’s estimates is very similar to the
posterior distribution P (X = x|K) (Griffiths & Tenenbaum, 2006; Vul et al., 2014).
More formally, we can say that as the number of adjustments t increases, the
distribution of estimates Q(x̂t ) converges to the posterior distribution P (X|K). This
model of computation has the property that each adjustment decreases an upper bound

model of mental computation in the domain of numerical estimation: First, the success
of MCMC methods in statistics, machine learning, and artificial intelligence suggests

they are well suited for the complex inference problems people face in everyday life.
Second, MCMC can explain important aspects of cognitive phenomena ranging from
category learning (Sanborn, Griffiths, & Navarro, 2010) to the temporal dynamics of

       Figure 3 illustrates this equation showing how the expected error cost – which
decays geometrically with the number of adjustments–and the time cost – which
increases linearly – determine the optimal speed-accuracy tradeoff. We inspected the
solution to Equation 2 when the belief and the proposal distribution are standard

found that for a wide range of realistic time costs the optimal number of adjustments

after the optimal number of adjustments is still biased towards the anchor as shown in
the bottom panel of Figure 4. This is a consequence of the geometric convergence of the

adjustments. This is a general property of this rational model of adjustment that can

problems according to their prevalence in the agent’s environment; for more information

adjustment makes the interesting, empirically testable prediction that the less time and

       Next we simulated the anchoring experiment by Russo and Schoemaker (1989).
In this experiment business students were first asked about the last three digits of their
telephone number. Upon hearing the number the experimenter announced he would add
400 to this number (providing an anchor) and proceeded to ask the participant whether
the year in which Attila the Hun was defeated in Europe was smaller or larger than
that sum. When the participant indicated her judgment, she was prompted to estimate
the year in which Attila had actually been defeated. Russo and Schoemaker (1989) then
compared the mean estimate between participants whose anchor had been 500 ± 100,
700 ± 100, · · · , 1300 ± 100. They found that their participants’ mean estimates
increased linearly with the provided anchor even though the correct value was A.D. 451.

       To simulate this experiment, we determined the values of µ and σ by the
elicitation method described above. Since the variability of people’s estimates and
confidence intervals was very high, we increased the sample size of this one experiment
to 200. We set the model parameters to the values estimated from the provided anchor
experiments by Jacowitz and Kahneman (1995) (see above). As Figure 10 shows, our
model correctly predicted that people’s estimates increase linearly with the provided
anchor (Russo & Schoemaker, 1989). To determine whether the quantitative differences
between the model predictions and the data reported by Russo and Schoemaker (1989)
were due to differences between business students in 1989 and people working on
Mechanical Turk in 2014, we ran an online replication of their experiment on
Mechanical Turk with 300 participants. There appeared to be no significant difference
between the estimates of the two populations. However, people’s estimates were highly
variable. Consequently, the error bars on the mean estimates are very large.

       Taking into account the high variance in people’s judgments, our simulation
results are largely consistent with the empirical data. In particular, both Russo and
Shoemaker’s data and our replication confirm our model’s qualitative prediction that
