Our analysis of optimal resource-allocation shows that, for a wide range of
plausible costs of computation, the resource-rational number of adjustments is much
smaller than the number of adjustments required for convergence to the posterior
distribution. This might explain why people’s estimates of unknown quantities are
biased towards their anchor across a wide range of circumstances. Yet, optimal resource
allocation also entails that the number of adjustments increases with the relative cost of
error and decreases with the relative cost of time. Hence, our theory predicts that the
anchoring bias is smaller when errors are costly and larger when time is costly; Figure
6b illustrates this prediction.

       Although we derived the implications of making rational use of finite cognitive
resources for a specific computational mechanism based on sampling, the crucial
property of diminishing returns per additional computation is a universal feature of
iterative inference mechanisms including approximate Bayesian computation (Sunnåker
anchoring experiments violate people’s expectation that the experimenter will provide
relevant information, provide negligible incentives for accuracy, and ask people to
estimate quantities about which they know very little.

       There also is empirical evidence suggesting that people do not always use the
provided value as their anchor. For instance, in the experiment by Strack and
Mussweiler (1997) the provided anchor influenced the participants’ estimates only when
it was semantically related to the quantity to be estimated. Pohl (1998) found that the
anchoring bias was absent when the anchor was perceived as implausible, and Hardt
and Pohl (2003) found that the bias was smaller on trials where the anchor’s judged
plausibility was below the median plausibility judgment. Thus, at least under some
circumstances, people appear to discard the provided value when it appears irrelevant
or misleading.

       However, realizing that the provided anchor is implausible and generating a
better anchor require knowledge, effort, and time. Therefore, when people are asked to
estimate a quantity they know almost nothing about, it may be resource-rational for
them to anchor on whatever the experimenter suggested. This seems applicable to most
anchoring experiments, because participants are usually so uncertain that they do not
even know in which direction to adjust from the provided anchor (Simmons et al.,
2010). If you cannot even tell whether the correct value is larger or smaller than the
anchor, how could you generate a better one? The effect of the anchor is largest in
people with little knowledge and high uncertainty about the quantity to be estimated
(Jacowitz & Kahneman, 1995; Wilson et al., 1996). These people would benefit from a
better anchor, but they cannot easily generate one, because they lack the relevant

knowledge. Conversely, our simulation of the effect of knowledge suggested that people
knowledgeable enough to generate good anchors, will perform well even if they start
from a highly implausible anchor. Although this argument is speculative and has yet to
be made precise it suggests that, at least in some situations, self-generating an anchor
might not be worth the effort regardless of one’s knowledge.

Function. In numerical estimation people have to make an informed guess
about an unknown quantity X based on their knowledge K. In general, people’s
relevant knowledge K is incomplete and insufficient to determine the quantity X with
certainty. For instance, people asked to estimate the boiling point of water on Mount
Everest typically do not know its exact value, but they do know related information,
such as the boiling point of water at normal altitude, the freezing point of water, the
qualitative relationship between altitude, air pressure, and boiling point, and so on. We
formalize people’s uncertain belief about X by the probability distribution P (X|K)
which assigns a plausibility p(X = x|K) to each potential value x. According to
Bayesian decision theory, the goal is to report the estimate x̂ with the highest expected
utility EP (X|K) [u(x̂, x)]. This is equivalent to finding the estimate with the lowest

    While the assumption above may be an overly restrictive one, we emphasize that this assumption
is not necessary for our model. For example, with multiple confidence judgments per individual, one
can assign a separate prior uncertainty parameter for each category, even when the target dimension
Hk is not the same. To do so, we only require that the confidence judgments be related to one another
in some meaningful way. For example, one could assume that the different confidence judgments
come from the same overarching process, so that when a confidence judgment of ‘‘1” is provided
for the estimate in Question k, it will be related to a confidence judgment of ‘‘1” in Question l. As
another example, one could assume a functional form (e.g., a linear relationship) for how the confi-
dence judgments are related to the prior uncertainty. As a result, having information about other con-
fidence judgments such as ‘‘1” and ‘‘4” will inform our estimates of confidence judgments such as ‘‘3”,
even if this judgment was never actually elicited in the experiment.
    In an attempt to create a more parsimonious model, we now discuss a way to relate the influence
that a given anchor value may have to the anchor’s consistency with an individual’s prior
representation.


5.2. Prior consistency
5.3.2. The mapping function
    We next define a mapping function to relate the prior consistency variable w to the influence of the
anchor parameter k. In theory, this function may be very complex, requiring many parameters to
relate the two variables precisely for all participants. However, in practice, this function should posit
psychologically meaningful parameters and will likely require some simplifying assumptions to facil-
itate the interpretability of these parameters.
    For simplicity, AIM assumes that as the distance between the prior representation and the anchor
increases, the anchor provides a marginally decreasing influence on the posterior representation, pro-
ducing an inverted U-shaped relationship between anchor extremity and the magnitude of the shift
from prior to posterior representation. This assumption is informed by the inverted U-shaped relation-
ship observed by Wegener et al. (2001). That said, there are potential special cases where this assump-
tion may not hold. First, if an individual uses an anchor as a hint (Schwarz, 1994; Wegener et al., 2010)
it is feasible to assume that the hint is an exaggeration. If a speaker states that it was ‘‘1,000,000
degrees outside,” the listener may infer that it is ‘‘very hot” outside, as opposed to it actually being
‘‘1,000,000 degrees.” Thus, the anchor would act as a more plausible exemplar (e.g., 125 degrees).
Other anchors (e.g., 500,000 and 1,500,000 degrees) would produce similar effects, resulting in an
asymptoting, rather than inverted-U, relationship between anchor extremity and the size of anchoring
effects (Mussweiler & Strack, 2001). AIM can capture this asymptoting behavior through the param-
eter kmax . Another special case could occur when an individual has no prior information about a target
item. If there is no prior representation, then the posterior representation will be made up entirely of

This allows the model to infer how confidence may relate to uncertainty across both items and par-
ticipants. Second, we use a measure of prior consistency to relate the influence of an anchor to a par-
ticipant’s prior information. In sum, as an anchor becomes more inconsistent with a participant’s
information (i.e., becomes more implausible), our AIM assumes that the anchor will have a propor-

Experiment 1 was intended to test the model across a range of judgment targets and a wide variety
of anchoring effects. The following sections will demonstrate the etiologies of regular anchoring
effects, directional anchors, irrelevant anchors, and the influence of cognitive load on anchoring
effects.


4.1. Methods

    Participants were recruited from Amazon’s Mechanical Turk website (see Buhrmester, Kwang, &
Gosling, 2011; Paolacci, Chandler, & Ipeirotis, 2010, for a review of Mechanical Turk as a viable source
of experimental data) and completed the task in exchange for $0.50. A total of 589 participants (sub
sample information will be provided by condition) completed one of the five between-participant con-
ditions: prior, regular anchors, directional anchors, irrelevant anchors, and cognitive load.
                                  B.M. Turner, D.R. Schley / Cognitive Psychology 90 (2016) 1–47                             13


4.1.1. Materials
    Participants in every condition were presented the same 6 anchoring problems taken from
Simmons et al. (2010) and Jacowitz and Kahneman (1995). The six target questions were as follows:
(1) the length of the Mississippi River, (2) the average annual rainfall in Philadelphia, (3) the maximum
speed of a house cat, (4) the average annual temperature of Phoenix, (5) the population of Chicago, and
(6) the height of the tallest redwood tree. Once the correct answer was determined, for some questions
we set anchors that were either higher or lower than the true value. Questions 1, 3, and 5 used high
anchors (3500 miles, 55 miles per hour, and 5 million people, respectively) whereas Questions 2, 4,
and 6 used low anchors (25 in., 52 °F, and 65 feet, respectively).

4.1.2. Procedure
    The five between-participant conditions are outlined in Table 1. In all conditions participants esti-
mated each of the six target items. Thus, Experiment 1 employed a 5 between-participant (Anchoring
Condition)  6 within-participant (Target Questions) mixed design. In addition to the prior (i.e., unan-
chored control condition) and regular anchor conditions, we included three additional anchoring para-
digms that have received notable attention within the anchoring literature. Because anchors often
provide directional information we included a condition with directional anchors (Simmons et al.,
2010). The literature on irrelevant anchors and numeric primes has been controversial to say the least,
with evidence toward (Adaval & Monroe, 2002; Critcher & Gilovich, 2008; Englich, 2008;
Oppenheimer et al., 2008; Mussweiler & Englich, 2005; Wilson et al., 1996; Wong & Kwong, 2000)
and against (Brewer & Chapman, 2002; Chapman & Johnson, 1994; Frederick & Mochon, 2012;
Mochon & Frederick, 2013; Mussweiler & Strack, 2001) such effects. As such, we included a condition
where the anchors were in reference to items different than those of the target judgments. Lastly,
6. Experiment 2

    The primary goal of Experiment 2 was to test AIM’s ability to account for empirical data on an indi-
vidual participant basis. Experiment 2 employed a within-participant anchoring design to investigate
how individuals integrate prior information and information provided by the anchor in the formation
of a posterior judgment. Employing a within-participant design will provide the conditions necessary
to fully identify the model we presented above.

6.1. Methods

   Participants were recruited from Amazon’s Mechanical Turk website and completed the task in
exchange for $0.50. The sample (N = 189) was 52% female with a mean age of 35 years. Participants
completed a similar task to the regular anchors condition of Experiment 1. For each of the six ques-
tions from Experiment 1, the task began by eliciting an unanchored (i.e., prior) judgment about the
target item and corresponding confidence rating for this first judgment, from 1 (Very Unconfident)
to 13 (Very Confident). After completing this first task, participants completed roughly 15 min worth
of unrelated non-numeric (to avoid the possibility of incidental anchors) tasks aimed at decreasing
the accessibility of participants’ unanchored judgments within their memories. Subsequently, partic-
ipants were presented the anchor in a comparison question (e.g., is the length of the Mississippi River
greater than or less than 3500 miles?) before estimating the target and providing a confidence judg-
ment the second time for each of the six items.

6.2. The model

    In contrast to Experiment 1, in Experiment 2 participants elicited an estimate from their prior rep-
us in selecting how the anchor might influence an individual’s estimate. We draw from assumptions
commonly made in categorization and similarity models. These models assume that as stimuli are
presented, they activate internal representations of categories as a function of their distance from
the perceived stimuli (e.g., Kruschke, 1992; Nosofsky, 1986). The further these perceptions are from
the category representations, the less active the internal category becomes, which results in a decrease
in the likelihood of that particular classification. Unlike categorization models, AIM assumes a contin-
uous internal representation for the ‘‘classification” of the true state of h0 . AIM assumes that the
anchor possesses information about h0 that influences the internal representation. Clearly, some
anchors will have a stronger influence on an individual’s representation than others. To accommodate
this feature, the information function can take many forms depending on the value of an ‘‘anchor influ-
ence” parameter k. Because of the explicit dependence of the information function on the anchor a and
the anchor influence parameter k, we denote the information function InfoðHja; kÞ.
    We will again assume that the influence of the anchor has a convenient functional form. The form
of the information function will take one of two distributions, depending on whether or not the anchor
provides directional information. For anchors that do not provide directional information, we assume
that the information function is normally distributed with mean equal to the anchor a and standard
deviation equal to k, such that

    AIM’s assumptions about the influence of the anchor are made mostly out of convenience. Specif-
ically, by using a normal information function concurrently with a normal prior representation, we can
provide closed form expressions for the posterior representation, which is convenient for estimation
purposes. Notice that for directional anchors, the information function is not a probability distribution
(i.e., it does not integrate to one). However, as we show below, we do not require the information func-
tion to be a probability distribution due to the integration step used to derive the posterior represen-
tation. Specifying the information function in this way allows us to compare the parameter k across a
variety of anchor types (e.g., regular and directional).

3.3. The posterior representation

    The final component of the model is the posterior representation. Similar to the prior representa-
tion, the posterior representation is a distribution over H, and reflects the underlying beliefs about h0
following the presentation of the anchor value a. The posterior representation serves as the final result
of the integration of a priori information (i.e., the prior representation) and information provided by
the anchor. There are many ways in which the prior representation could be combined with the infor-
mation function to form this new posterior representation.5 One convenient and normative way to
combine two distributions is through Bayes’ rule.
    We denote the posterior representation as PostðHjh; d; a; kÞ, and we obtain it by multiplying the
prior representation PriorðHjh; dÞ by the information function InfoðHja; kÞ and marginalizing, such that

Judgment and Decision Making, Vol. 16, No. 1, January 2021, pp. 131–141




 Anchoring without scale distortion

 Štěpán Bahník∗



 Abstract

 The scale distortion theory of anchoring argues that people are inﬂuenced by a
 previously considered numeric value, an anchor, because the anchor distorts the scale
 on which a subsequent judgment is made. The distortion of the scale due to the anchor
 is a momentary eﬀect that would be overridden if the scale was distorted again, for
 example, by consideration of a diﬀerent value on the same scale. In the present study,
 participants compared thirteen random anchors on the same scale to thirteen diﬀerent
 objects. Subsequent numeric estimates of objects’ attributes were inﬂuenced by the
 corresponding anchors even though the anchors were divided from the estimates by
 twelve questions pertaining to diﬀerent values on the same scale. The numeric value
 considered immediately before the estimate did not have a considerable eﬀect on the
 judgment. While the anchoring eﬀect was robust, it cannot be easily explained by
 scale distortion. Other possible theories of the anchoring eﬀect are compatible with
 the results.
 Keywords: anchoring, scale distortion, judgment



 time in advance.

 2.2 Materials
 The study consisted of two parts. In the ﬁrst part of the study, participants were given 13
 objects that they compared with a random anchor. The objects were selected to be either
 known to the participants (e.g., related to well-known Prague locations) or speciﬁed in a
 way that their characteristics could be reasonably estimated (e.g., “highest waterfall Angel
 Falls”). For each item, participants ﬁrst generated a random number and then answered
 whether the given object was smaller or larger in terms of size in meters than the generated
 random number. The dimension of size was always speciﬁed to be length, height, or
 distance. The random generation was emphasized by a mechanism similar to a slot machine
 with three “wheels”, each with a single digit, that spun and then stopped on the number of

CONSIDERING THE IMPOSSIBLE:
EXPLAINING THE EFFECTS OF
IMPLAUSIBLE ANCHORS
Thomas Mussweiler and Fritz Strack
Universität Würzburg




Research on judgmental anchoring - the assimilation of a numeric estimate towards
a previously considered standard - has demonstrated that implausible anchors pro-
duce large effects. We propose an insufficient adjustment plus selective accessibil-
ity account for these effects. Specifically, judges may adjust from an implausible
anchor until a plausible value for the target is reached and may then test the hypoth-
esis that the target’s extension is similar to this value. If this is indeed the case, then
differentially extreme implausible anchors should produce similar absolute esti-
mates, because adjustment from any implausible anchor should terminate at the
same value. Results of two studies are consistent with this prediction. They show
that implausible anchors that differ extremely produce similar absolute estimates.
The implications of these findings for alternative models of anchoring are dis-
cussed.

Human judgment under uncertainty is often influenced by salient
judgmental anchors. In what is probably the best known demonstra-
tion of such anchoring effects (Tversky & Kahneman, 1974), partici-
pants first received a comparative judgment task in which they were
asked whether the percentage of African nations in the UN is higher
or lower than an arbitrary number (the anchor) that had been deter-
mined by spinning a wheel of fortune (i.e., 65% or 10%). In the subse-
quent absolute judgment task, participants were asked to give their

RESULTS AND DISCUSSION

Inspection of the means given in Table 1 reveals that the expected
pattern was obtained. Although the two implausible anchors dif-
fered much more from one another than the two plausible ones, the
difference in the resulting absolute estimates was much larger for the
plausible than the implausible anchors.
 In a 2 (Anchor: high vs. low) X 2 (Plausibility: plausible vs. im-
plausible) ANOVA using the absolute estimates as the dependent
variable, this pattern was borne out in a significant interaction ef-
fect, F(1, 59) = 4.39, p < .04. In this analysis the main effect of Plausi-
bility was also significant, F(1,59) = 4.81, p < .03, and the main effect
of Anchor proved to be marginal, F(1, 59) = 3.29, p < .08. An analysis
of the simple effects further revealed that the difference between
the high and the low anchor condition was only significant for the
plausible anchors, t(30) = 2.78, p < .01, and not for the implausible
ones, t(29) = .2, p > .8.
 This finding provides initial evidence in support of our conceptu-
alization. It demonstrates that the pattern of estimates corresponds

with the predictions derived from our model. To demonstrate the
ability of our findings to be generalized, we attempted to replicate
this finding with a different content domain (i.e., the age of Mahatma
Gandhi) and with implausible anchors that were less extreme than
the ones used in Study 1.

STUDY 2
METHOD

 Participants. 109 male and female non-psychology students at the
University of Würzburg participated in what was ostensibly a pre-
test for the construction of a general knowledge questionnaire. They
were randomly assigned to one of the four experimental conditions.
 Materials and Procedure. The questionnaire consisted of four pairs
of comparative and absolute questions which were similar to those
used in Study 1. The critical question pair pertained to the age of Ma-
hatma Gandhi (“Was Mahatma Gandhi younger or older than X
years when he died?,” and “How old was Mahatma Gandhi?”) and
was taken from a pool of questions we used in our earlier research
(Strack & Mussweiler, 1997). The low plausible anchor (61 years) was
one standard deviation below the mean estimate of our calibration
sample (N = 151). The high plausible anchor (86 years) was one stan-
dard deviation above that mean. The two implausible anchors (214
and 271 years) were about 18 and 26 standard deviations above the
mean. Mahatma Gandhi actually died at the age of 78. The procedure
was identical to that used in Study 1.

RESULTS AND DISCUSSION
Inspection of the means given in Table 2 reveals the expected pattern.
Again, the difference between absolute estimates that resulted for
the high and low anchors, was larger for the plausible than for the im-
plausible anchors.
 In a 2 (Anchor: high vs. low) X 2 (Plausibility: plausible vs. implau-

3.84, p < .05. In this analysis, the main effect for Plausibility also
reached significance, F(1, 105) = 8.73, p < .004, whereas the main effect

ORGANIZATIONAL BEHAVIOR AND HUMAN DECISION PROCESSES 39, 84-97 (1987)




 Experts, Amateurs, and Real Estate: An Anchoring-and-
 Adjustment Perspective on Property Pricing Decisions
 GREGORY B. NORTHCFCAFTANDMARGARET A. NEALE
 Department of Management and Policy, University of Arizona

 The studies described in this paper investigated the use of a decisional heu-
 ristic-anchoring-and-adjustment-in an information-rich, real world setting.
 In order to assess the generalizability of laboratory research on this decision
 heuristic, students and real estate agents toured and made pricing decisions
 about real estate properties. It was hypothesized that manipulated listing
 prices would anchor values assigned to the properties. Results were consis-
 tent with the use of an anchoring-and-adjustment value estimation strategy in
 information-rich, real world settings. Implications for the understanding of
 judgmental expertise are discussed. Q 1987 Academic Press, Inc.

 Interest in the relevance of behavioral decision theory and laboratory-
documented cognitive biases to real world decision behavior has in-
creased markedly over the last 10 years. Recently, researchers (Berkeley
& Humphreys, 1982; Hogarth, 1981; Winkler & Murphy, 1973) have sug-
gested that the demonstration of decisional biases is a function of the
contrived nature of the laboratory setting or the decisional demands of
laboratory experiment participation. Much of the research on decision
bias is based upon individuals making decisions under the controlled and
“degraded” or informationally impoverished conditions of the laboratory
(e.g., Kahneman & Tversky, 1972, 1979; Tversky, 1972; Tversky & Kah-
neman, 1973). It has been hypothesized that, as with “perceptual illu-
sions” in experimental psychology (Neisser, 1976) which disappear once
the subject is allowed to interact with the object, decisional biases also
may disappear once decision makers are placed in the information-rich
context in which actual decisions are made. The studies described in this
paper investigated the biasing potential of one particular decisional heu-
ristic-anchoring-and-adjustment-in an information-rich, real world
setting.

 This project was supported in part by NSF Grant IST-8408717, “Experts vs. Amateurs:
The Role of Expertise in Human Information Processing and Decision Behavior.” The au-
thors thank Katherine Martin of Tucson Realty and Trust, and Jennifer Bortz, Pauline
Johnson, Caroline O’Reilly, and Laurie Topp for their assistance in this research. Corre-
spondence concerning this manuscript, including requests for reprints, should be directed to

Playing Dice With Criminal Sentences: The Influence of
Irrelevant Anchors on Experts’ Judicial Decision Making
Birte Englich
University of Würzburg
Thomas Mussweiler
University of Cologne
Fritz Strack
University of Würzburg
One of the most intriguing instances of irrelevant
influences on human judgment is that of a preceding
judgment. Research on the so-called anchoring effect
has demonstrated that a randomly chosen standard in a
comparative judgment task may dramatically influence a
subsequent absolute judgment of the same target. Indicating whether the percentage of African nations in the
United Nations is higher or lower than an arbitrary number (the anchor) that has been determined by spinning a
wheel of fortune (showing 65% or 10%), for example,
influences subsequent estimates of this percentage
(Tversky & Kahneman, 1974). Specifically, absolute
judgments are assimilated toward the randomly chosen
“anchor values.” Such anchoring effects pervade a plethora of judgments (e.g., Epley & Gilovich, 2001;
Northcraft & Neale, 1987) and are remarkably robust.
Many findings indicate that clearly irrelevant numbers—
even if they are blatantly determined at random—may
guide numeric judgments that are generated under
uncertainty (for an overview, see Chapman & Johnson,

content.content:
Journal of Experimental Social Psychology 35, 136–164 (1999)
Article ID jesp.1998.1364, available online at http://www.idealibrary.com on

Hypothesis-Consistent Testing and Semantic Priming in the
Anchoring Paradigm: A Selective Accessibility Model
Thomas Mussweiler
Northwestern University

and
Fritz Strack
Universität Würzburg, Würzburg, Germany
Received June 11, 1998; Revised July 3, 1998; Accepted July 15, 1998
Results of four studies support the notion that anchoring effects are mediated by
mechanisms of hypothesis-consistent testing and semantic priming. According to the
suggested Selective Accessibility Model, judges use a hypothesis-consistent test strategy to
solve a comparative anchoring task. Applying this strategy selectively increases the
accessibility of anchor-consistent knowledge which is then used to generate the subsequent
absolute judgment. Studies 1 and 2 demonstrate that absolute estimates depend on the
hypothesis implied in the comparative task, suggesting that a hypothesis-testing strategy is
used to solve this task. Study 3 shows that limiting the amount of knowledge generated for
the comparative task retards absolute judgments. This suggests that knowledge rendered
easily accessible in the comparative judgment is used for the subsequent absolute
judgment. Finally, Study 4 suggests that self-generation of knowledge contributes to the
robustness of the effect, thus resolving the seeming inconsistency that anchoring effects are
at the same time remarkably robust and mediated by typically fragile semantic priming
mechanisms. r 1999 Academic Press
Key Words: anchoring heuristic; selective accessibility; hypothesis-consistent testing;
semantic priming.
The present research was supported by a grant from the Deutsche Forschungsgemeinschaft. We
thank Russell Fazio, John Skowronski, Timothy Wilson, Bob Wyer, and an anymous reviewer for
helpful and extensive comments on an earlier draft of this manuscript. Thanks also go to Jens Förster,
Roland Neumann, Sabine Stepper and Lioba Werth for discussions of the issue, to Markus Denzler,

Weiss for their assistance in data collection and to Jens Unger for the computer programming. Finally,
we want to thank Gerd Bohner for giving methodological advice.

Anchoring. Fifty-four anchoring questions were developed to measure the tendency to
overweight an initially considered piece of information when making a judgment. Forty-two of

 DEBIASING THROUGH OBSERVATIONAL LEARNING

14

these items were numerical anchoring items. They asked participants to make numerical
estimates in the presence of an anchor that was either provided or self-generated, and either
relevant or irrelevant for the judgment at hand (Simmons et al., 2010; Strack & Mussweiler,
1997; Tversky & Kahneman, 1974). Items were scored by calculating the distance between a
participant’s estimate and the correct answer, divided by the distance between the anchor and the
correct answer. These scores varied between 0 and 1, with lower scores indicating more biased
answers. Estimates that exceeded the value of the correct answer in the direction away from the
anchor were scored as 1. Estimates that exceed the value of the anchor in the direction away
from the correct answer were scored as 0 (see Figure 1).

Figure 1. Scoring of answers by relative distance between the anchor and the correct answer.

Twelve additional items assessed focalism by asking participants to forecast their
happiness in a hypothetical future situation, and then to revise their initial estimate based on a
consideration of the daily activities they would undertake in that situation (Schkade &
Kahneman, 1998; Wilson, Lindsey, & Schooler, 2000). Items were scored as the difference
between the predicted happiness ratings and the revised happiness ratings. The difference was
rescaled to vary between 0 and 1, such that cases in which the revised happiness ratings were
equal to the predicted happiness ratings (indicating minimum susceptibility to focalism bias)
were scored as 1, and cases in which the two ratings were maximally different (indicating
maximum susceptibility to focalism bias) were scored as 0.

deviations.md:30:- **Unit mismatch removed by the gross-error rule (Q15) and eligibility re-check (Q14).** In Shanks et al. (2020, Study 3), "Population of Chicago", participants answered in millions (median 2.6) while the true value (2,746,388) and anchors (200,000; 5,000,000) are raw counts. All 870 valid responses in that cell exceed the gross-error limit, so the cell drops out of the across-cell set (129 design cells, 128 analysed). The other 117 responses removed as gross errors come from 13 studies (including 6 responses to other items of the same Shanks et al. study), mostly Freira et al. (2020, Study 4), a forecast of US COVID-19 deaths made early in the pandemic, and Weber et al. (2021), "Shortest distance between Russia and USA", whose true value is a few kilometres.
prereg/preregistration.md:76:- A 2026 corrigendum to Weber & Röseler (2025; OSF component sz5b9) reports item-to-effect mix-ups in their study. Weber et al. (2021) contributes 14 cells to the across-cell set. Whether the OpAQ master file is affected is unknown (robustness analysis R6).
prereg/preregistration.md:142:- R6: H2 without Weber et al. (2021).

SUSCEPTILITY TO ANCHORING EFFECTS

Testing the Reliability of Anchoring Susceptibility Scores
Lucia Weber1 and Lukas Röseler2

1

Faculty of Medicine, University of Zurich, Switzerland

2

Münster Center for Open Science, University of Münster, Germany

Author Note
Lucia Weber
Lukas Röseler

https://orcid.org/0000-0002-6446-1901

Correspondence concerning this article should be addressed to Lukas Röseler, University
of Münster. Email: [email redacted]

Preprint Version
This manuscript corresponds to the corrected version of the article published in EJOP
(February 2025). This manuscript has not been peer reviewed in this form.

 SUSCEPTIBILITY TO ANCHORING EFFECTS

Abstract
Whereas anchoring is a very robust and well-known effect that refers to the assimilation of
numeric estimates toward previously considered numbers, the psychological mechanisms
behind it have yet to be fully clarified. Research on theories on how susceptibility to
anchoring is related to other personality parameters has not been able to provide sufficient
empirical evidence of such relationships. A probable explanation is that anchoring scores lack
reliability in most anchoring experiments. The present research examined whether reliability
depends on the type of score used to capture anchoring susceptibility. In a classical anchoring
experiment, men and women aged between 14 and 67 years (N = 78) were asked to estimate
the true values of certain numbers (e.g., height of the Zugspitze mountain) after being
confronted with either a high or a low anchor number. Four different anchoring scores that are
commonly used to measure susceptibility to anchoring in anchoring research were computed

attachment.snippet: 1 # Extreme anchors lose proportional pull: A preregistered, model-based test of how anchoring scales with anchor extremity in open trial-level data 2 Lukas Wallrich 3 4 **Abstract** 5 6 Anchors bias numeric estimates, but it is unclear whether an anchor’s 7 proportional influence rises, stays constant or falls as the anchor 8 becomes more extreme. Meta-analyses report larger standardised effects 9 for more distant anchors, yet a standardised mean difference rises with 10 anchor distance even when the proportional pull is constant. We derived 11 the shape of the anchor-response function from five process models 12 (anchor-and-adjust with a fixed or a resource-rational number of 13 adjustments, constant-weight integration, adjustment to the edge of the 14 plausible range, and plausibility-discounted integration), simulated 15 them on the designs of the Open Anchoring Quest, and preregistered the 16 predictions before reading any estimates. In 20 item-study cells with at 17 least three anchor values (7,949 estimates, mostly random anchors), the 18 log-scale elasticity of estimates with respect to anchors averaged 0.31 19 and fell as anchors moved away from the true value (curvature -0.041, 20 95% CI \[-0.058, -0.023\]; relative curvature -0.13). This contradicts 21 anchor-and-adjust with a fixed number of adjustments and constant-weight 22 integration. Across 128 two-anchor cells from 40 studies, the anchoring 23 index did not change detectably with extremity (slope 0.050, \[-0.013, 24 0.113\]). Only the resource-rational variant, whose predictions were 25 least constrained, survived the preregistered model checks. Proportional 26 anchor influence declines within items, whereas comparisons across items 27 with researcher-chosen anchors do not show this decline. 28 29 **Keywords:** anchoring, anchor extremity, process models, resource 30 rationality, secondary data analysis, preregistration 31 32 # Introduction 33 34 Numeric judgements are drawn towards numbers people have just 35 considered. In the classic demonstration, participants who first judged 36 whether the percentage of African countries in the United Nations was 37 higher or lower than a random number gave estimates that moved towards 38 that number (Tversky & Kahneman, 1974). The effect appears with 39 arbitrary and informative anchors, with lay people and experts, and in 40 consequential settings such as property valuation and criminal 41 sentencing (Englich et al., 2006; Furnham & Boo, 2011; Northcraft & 42 Neale, 1987). A meta-analysis of openly shared trial-level data from 90 43 anchoring studies estimated a pooled standardised effect of *g* = 0.69 44 (Röseler et al., 2022; Röseler & Schütz, 2022). 45 46 Whether an anchor’s influence depends on how extreme it is has practical 47 and theoretical weight. Practically, negotiators, litigants and survey 48 designers choose anchor values, and whether an extreme opening offer 49 buys proportionally more influence than a moderate one depends on this 50 relation. Theoretically, the leading accounts of anchoring make 51 different predictions about this question, so the shape of the relation 52 between anchor extremity and anchor influence is one of the few places 53 where they can be tested against each other. 54 55 ## Evidence on anchor extremity 56 57 Experiments that varied anchor extremity have produced mixed results. 58 Chapman & Johnson (1994) found that “implausibly extreme anchors had a 59 proportionally smaller effect than anchors close to the expected value” 60 in lottery valuations. Strack & Mussweiler (1997) found that implausible 61 anchors produced a larger raw shift in estimates than plausible ones. 62 When implausible anchors were placed far beyond the plausible range, 63 estimates under them were no higher than estimates under a plausible 64 high anchor (Mussweiler & Strack, 2001), and Wegener et al. (2001) found 65 that very extreme anchors had smaller effects than moderate ones. These 66 studies compared two to four anchor levels, mostly for a handful of 67 items. The most fine-grained test so far used a perceptual task: Imhoff 68 & Barker (2023, Study 2) showed participants dot patterns of about 500 69 dots next to standards labelled with their exact number of dots, which 70 differed from the target by up to 400 dots in 20-dot steps. Estimates 71 were drawn towards these symbolic anchors, but the pull levelled off 72 once the anchor differed from the target by more than about 300 dots. 73 74 The two recent meta-analyses reach different conclusions. Using the Open 75 Anchoring Quest (OpAQ) data, Röseler & Schütz (2022) found that Hedges’ 76 *g* increased with the relative distance between anchor and true value 77 and concluded against the prediction that extreme anchors produce 78 smaller effects. Schley & Weingarten (2026) coded extremity as a binary 79 flag for anchors that the original authors described as extreme and 80 found no difference in effect size. Barrera-Lemarchand et al. (2024) 81 modelled the anchored crowd mean as a weighted average of anchor and 82 crowd mean, with a weight that decays exponentially with the distance 83 between anchor and truth, and found that this weight fell with distance 84 across 30 percentage questions. 85 86 These results are hard to compare because they measure anchor influence 87 in different units. A standardised mean difference between high- and 88 low-anchor conditions rises with the distance between the anchors even 89 if every anchor pulls estimates by the same proportion of its distance. 90 A finding that *g* grows with anchor distance is therefore compatible 91 with constant, rising and falling proportional influence. The theories 92 speak to the proportional pull: how much of the distance between belief 93 and anchor is carried into the estimate. Jacowitz & Kahneman (1995) 94 captured this with the anchoring index, the difference between median 95 estimates under high and low anchors divided by the difference between 96 the anchors, and Röseler & Schütz (2022) called for such a unitless 97 measure “to formalize the relationship between anchor distance and 98 adjustment strength”. 99 100 ## Process models and their predictions 101 102 We consider five process models. Each maps an anchor and a belief onto 103 an estimate, and each implies a shape for the relation between anchor 104 extremity and proportional pull 105 (Figure 1). 106 107 In *anchor-and-adjust with a fixed number of adjustments* (M1), people 108 start at the anchor and adjust towards their belief in a limited number 109 of stochastic steps. Lieder et al. (2018) formalised adjustment as a 110 Metropolis-Hastings chain that starts at the anchor and moves towards 111 the belief distribution. When the anchor is far away, each step covers a 112 bounded distance, so a fixed number of steps leaves a larger share of 113 the distance uncorrected, and the proportional pull rises with 114 extremity. Lieder et al. approximated the chain’s convergence as 115 geometric, which implies a constant proportional pull (their Eq. 4); 116 that approximation holds for anchors near the belief, and our 117 simulations use the chain itself. 118 119 In *resource-rational anchor-and-adjust* (M1R), the number of 120 adjustments is chosen to minimise expected error plus a time cost per 121 adjustment (Lieder et al., 2018, Eq. 2). Anchors inside the plausible 122 range are barely adjusted, because adjusting from them buys little 123 accuracy, while far anchors justify many adjustments. The resulting pull 124 can fall with extremity, but its shape depends on the time cost and on 125 how uncertain people are. 126 127 In *constant-weight integration* (M2), the estimate is a weighted 128 average of anchor and belief with a fixed weight. This is the simplest 129 version of the anchor integration model (Turner & Schley, 2016), and in 130 log units it implies a constant proportional pull. It is the null model 131 for shape. 132 133 In *adjustment to the plausible boundary* (M3), people accept anchors 134 that lie inside the range of values they find plausible and adjust from ... 84:Experiments that varied anchor extremity have produced mixed results. @chapman1994 found that "implausibly extreme anchors had a proportionally smaller effect than anchors close to the expected value" in lottery valuations. @strack1997 found that implausible anchors produced a larger raw shift in estimates than plausible ones. When implausible anchors were placed far beyond the plausible range, estimates under them were no higher than estimates under a plausible high anchor [@mussweiler2001], and @wegener2001 found that very extreme anchors had smaller effects than moderate ones. These studies compared two to four anchor levels, mostly for a handful of items. The most fine-grained test so far used a perceptual task: @imhoff2023 [Study 2] showed participants dot patterns of about 500 dots next to standards labelled with their exact number of dots, which differed from the target by up to 400 dots in 20-dot steps. Estimates were drawn towards these symbolic anchors, but the pull levelled off once the anchor differed from the target by more than about 300 dots.
114:We tested these predictions on OpAQ, an openly licensed collection of trial-level anchoring data [@roseler2022opaq]. Because anchor values in most studies were chosen by the original authors together with the items, a comparison across items confounds extremity with item properties. Our primary test is therefore within items: in studies that presented many different anchors for the same question, we asked how the proportional pull changes as the anchor moves away from the true value. Compared with the dot-estimation evidence of @imhoff2023, these studies use general-knowledge magnitudes and anchors that lie up to several orders of magnitude from the true value. A comparison of the anchoring index across two-anchor studies is a secondary test. We simulated every model on the exact OpAQ designs to derive numeric predictions and passed the simulated data through the same estimators as the observed data. We preregistered the predictions, decision rules and analyses before reading any estimate.
132:- **Within-item set** (primary): item-study cells with at least three distinct anchor values. It contains `r dc$within_cells` cells from `r dc$within_studies` studies (`r nf(dc$within_rows)` estimates, `r nf(dc$within_participants)` participants). Fifteen cells used random anchors: 13 general-knowledge items from @bahnik2021, in which each participant compared 13 random anchors between 1 and 1,000 to 13 lengths and heights, and two items from @yoon2021. Five cells used fixed anchors: four items with 10 high anchor levels each from unpublished data by Frech et al. (2021), contributed to OpAQ, and one item (the height of Cologne cathedral) with 20 anchor levels from a supplementary anchoring task in @imhoff2023 [Study 2].
247:*Dependence on single studies (H1).* Leaving out any one of the three smaller studies left the curvature negative with confidence intervals excluding zero (*g* from `r f3(min(s_("S2_without_Frech et al., 2021"), s_("S2_without_Yoon et al., 2021, Form C"), s_("S2_without_Imhoff & Barker, 2022, Study 2")))` to `r f3(max(s_("S2_without_Frech et al., 2021"), s_("S2_without_Yoon et al., 2021, Form C"), s_("S2_without_Imhoff & Barker, 2022, Study 2")))`). Adding study-level random effects gave *g* = `r f3(s_("S2_study_random_effect"))`, `r ci(s_("S2_study_random_effect", "lo"), s_("S2_study_random_effect", "hi"))`. The single fixed-anchor item with 20 anchor levels [the supplementary task of @imhoff2023, Study 2] showed a negative curvature on its own, *g* = `r f3(s_("S2_imhoff_barker_only"))`, `r ci(s_("S2_imhoff_barker_only", "lo"), s_("S2_imhoff_barker_only", "hi"))`.
257:The negative curvature contradicts two simple accounts. Anchor-and-adjust with a fixed number of steps predicts that far anchors keep more of their distance, because a bounded number of bounded steps cannot correct a large gap; the data show the reverse. Constant-weight integration, the simplest version of the anchor integration model, predicts no change in proportional pull; it too is contradicted. The accounts that predict a decline share one feature: the anchor's influence is limited by how plausible it is. This holds for adjustment that stops at the edge of the plausible range [@epley2006], for integration that discounts implausible anchors [@wegener2001; @turner2016], and for a resource-rational agent who invests more adjustments when the anchor is far off [@lieder2018a]. The result fits earlier experiments with few anchor levels in which implausible anchors had proportionally smaller effects [@chapman1994; @mussweiler2001; @wegener2001], the distance-decaying anchoring weight of @barrera2024, and the levelling-off of assimilation to symbolic anchors in dot estimation [@imhoff2023]. It extends these findings to general-knowledge magnitudes, to anchors far outside the plausible range, and to a proportional outcome. In a dot-estimation task with anchors 35% or 70% away from the true value, the more distant anchors produced larger estimation errors [@mayer2024]; a larger absolute effect is compatible with a declining proportional pull, so the two findings do not conflict.

the standard on the right, for the other half it was vice versa. In order to rule out confusion regarding
 which image to estimate, participants had to click a radio button to indicate what they thought the target
 image was (trials with wrong clicks were excluded). Different from the previous study, the nonsymbolic
 dot pattern of the standard was now accompanied by the symbolic numeric information displaying the
 actual number of dots presented in this standard (“This image contains [between 93 and 901] dots.”).
 A visual display of the trials can be found on OSF.
 For better use online and to reduce strain on participants, the DJT was shortened to include just
 41 trials per participant. In order to keep a similar granularity in measurement steps, however, 2
 counterbalancing conditions were created so that half of the participants were randomly assigned to
 either estimate 41 dot patterns of around 500 dots (±10 dots) next to standards that varied between
 400 dots above or below the target image in intervals of 20 dots. The second group judged 40 similar
 dot images in the presence of standards at each 20-dot-interval between 390 dots below or above
 the target image as well as one in which the both images had an equal number of dots. In effect,
 this counterbalancing offers the same 81-step precision in measurement that was also included in the
 previous study.

 3.1.3. Additional measures
 Again, some basic demographics were recorded, including age, sex, and education, although the
 INCOM was no longer administered in this study. An additional item was included at the start of the
 survey to check for correct image display by asking participants to describe what they saw on a simple
 image containing 3 shapes of different colors. A small traditional anchoring task, closely modeled on
 the task and one of the questions in Strack and Mussweiler’s work (1997), was also included after the
 main task for exploratory purposes not directly related to this line of research. This task and its analysis
 are described in detail in the additional materials available online. After this, an open-ended item
 was included to gauge participant’s suspicions regarding the goal of the current study. Finally, a new

 data-quality item was included in which participants were asked to indicate if their responses were
 made in earnest or not in order to increase the quality of the data in the ﬁnal analyses. Participants were
 guaranteed to not be affected in any way based on their responses to this item, but that it would help the
 researchers in their investigation if they responded honestly. Responses were given on a Likert scale
 ranging from “Deﬁnitely do not use my data” (1) to “Deﬁnitely use my data” (4). Responses of 2 or
 lower were taken as an indication of poor data-quality and used for the exclusion of participants from
 the analyses.

 3.1.4. Procedure
 Participants were fully informed about the data storage policy, procedure, and their rights before they
 were asked for their consent to take part in the study. After the image display check and demographics
 items participants completed 2 practice trails to get familiarized with the procedure of the main task.
 Randomly allocated to 1 of the 2 counter balancing conditions, participants completed the main batch of
 41 trials and afterward the traditional anchoring task. After this, the suspicion check item and the data-
 quality item were presented before participants were debriefed, thanked and given their compensation.
 The study lasted about 10 min.

 3.1.5. Data treatment
 Nonnumeric and empty responses made up 1% of trials while 0.7% showed a failed attention check
 leading to their exclusion. This time, responses that exceeded the maximum or minimum standard
 value (lower than 100 or higher than 900) were also removed (0.5%) to increase data quality, as such
 estimates are unlikely to be honest estimates as a clear reference was available. The remaining scores
 were z-transformed separately per participant to account for personal differences in response ranges.
 Z-scores above 3 or below −3, or instances where no z-score could be calculated were removed (e.g.,
 because participants always gave the same estimate, resulting in a denominator of zero), which was the
 case for 0.2% of trials. Due to co-occurrences of these criteria a total of 2.4% of the original trials were
 not used in the analyses. In addition, 12 participants indicated their data quality was low and should not
 be included in the analysis. Combined the exclusion criteria left a total of 790 participants with data
 suitable for use in the main analysis.


 3.2. Results
 Again, the main analysis took the form of a mixed model regression with REML that included ﬁxed
 effects for the number of dots present in the target, as well as the standard (and additionally given as
 a numeric anchor below the standard) in hundreds and modeled up to the third polynomials term. We
 included random slopes of the 3 polynomials as well as the actual number of dots for participants to
 account for participant level variation in patterns (no random intercept was estimated due to singular
 ﬁt issues). As in Study 1, participants were above-chance accurate in detecting subtle differences in the
 judged target stimulus (main effect of dots; Table 2). In addition, both the linear and cubic term of the
 comparison standard reached signiﬁcance in this analysis (Table 2), describing a pattern of assimilation
 in which the participants’ z-transformed estimates increased as the standards became more removed up
 until a difference of around 300 dots was reached, after which estimates remained stable (Figure 3).
 Thus, the provided symbolic anchor yielded an exclusively assimilative inﬂuence (leveled off toward
 extreme values) that completely overrode the contrastive inﬂuence of the (still present) nonsymbolic
 representation.
 As in the previous study, we conducted a second analysis adding 2 lagged predictors from the
 previous trials (the relative extremity of the standard as well as participants’ self-generated and

 inﬂuences from the previous trial. While a high response in the previous trial increased the estimate,

Study 2b

       In addition to the main DJT part of Study 2, a traditional anchoring paradigm was

included at the end of the work. The same participant, therefore, completed this study.

Method

       Task. Near the end of Study 2, the 803 participants from Study 02 were asked

whether the Cologne cathedral was higher or lower than some random anchor ranging from

10 to 390 meters in 20 meter intervals. Respondents then indicated whether they thought it

was higher or lower than this amount by using a radio button. As a follow up question

respondents were then asked to give their exact estimate for the height of the cathedral in

meters. These scores and the anchor values were then centred on the true size of the cathedral

(157 meters) so that score indicate the number of meters the response or anchor is removed

from the true answer.

       Data treatment. Twelve respondents indicated their data were of low quality and

were removed along with 16 non-numeric responses. Finally, one further scores above or

below 3 standard deviations from the average remaining responses were removed leaving 774

responses in total.

Results

       Orthogonal polynomials for the centred anchors up to the third term were regressed

on the centred scores, indicating a simple positive linear model best fit the data, t(770) =

8.96, β = 2009.54, 95% CI[1569.19, 2449.89], p < .001, with all other polynomial terms p >

.63. To give a more precise interpretation of the anchoring pattern, the simple linear model

was refit in isolation uncovering a clear assimilative pattern where each meter increase in the

anchor produced a 0.62meter increase in the response, t(772) = 8.97, β = 0.62, 95% CI[0.49,

0.76], p < .001, (Figure S1).
 Figure S1. Predicted responses in meters for each anchor step and predicted 95%CI.

Discussion

         In contrast to the findings in the main part of Study 02, the classical anchoring

paradigm did not show the expected levelling off of the anchoring effect even for the most

extreme anchors of 10 or 390 meters. The upward bound of which is more than twice as large

as the true value of the Cologne Cathedral (157 meters) and 10 meters taller than the Empire

State Building. It may still be that, due to the poor knowledge participants had of the

cathedral or other buildings, the anchors were not yet extreme enough to fall outside the

range of plausible values held by participants. Nevertheless, the findings here do not support

an insufficient adjustment account of anchoring and do not reproduce the findings on extreme

standards within a more classic anchoring paradigm that does not include sequential effects.

# Citation support check: manuscript.qmd

Checked 2026-09-28 against the current `manuscript.qmd` (including the `@imhoff2023` and `@mayer2024` citations). Each row is one (sentence, key) pair. Verdicts: SUPPORTED / PARTLY / NOT SUPPORTED / COULD NOT CHECK. Reference existence was not re-checked.

Sources read (full text unless stated): Tversky & Kahneman 1974 (Science PDF); Northcraft & Neale 1987; Englich et al. 2006; Furnham & Boo 2011 (scanned PDF, OCR); Röseler & Schütz 2022 preprint (osf.io/wf2tn); OpAQ data paper (jopd.67) and its correction (jopd.92); Chapman & Johnson 1994 (**abstract only**, from the academia.edu record; the full text could not be obtained); Strack & Mussweiler 1997; Mussweiler & Strack 1999; Mussweiler & Strack 2001; Wegener et al. 2001; Schley & Weingarten manuscript version; Barrera-Lemarchand et al. 2024 (accepted manuscript); Jacowitz & Kahneman 1995 (scanned PDF, OCR); Lieder et al. 2018a (PsyArXiv preprint and eScholarship copy of the published version; equation numbers are the same in both); Turner & Schley 2016; Epley & Gilovich 2006; Bahník 2021; Yoon et al. 2021 (accepted manuscript incl. Appendix A); Imhoff & Barker 2023 (article + online supplement "Study 2b"); Mayer & Rebholz 2024 preprint; Lakens 2017 (preprint); van den Akker et al. 2021. For Bahník, Yoon, Frech and Imhoff items, the OpAQ file (`data/raw/opaq_70a.csv`) and `output/design_cells.csv` were also used to identify which items enter the analysis.

| # | Location (section) | Key | Claim the citation must support | Verdict | Evidence / quote | Suggested fix |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Introduction ¶1 | tversky1974 | Participants judged whether the % of African countries in the UN was higher/lower than a random number; estimates moved towards it | SUPPORTED | p. 1128: "a number between 0 and 100 was determined by spinning a wheel of fortune in the subjects' presence. The subjects were instructed to indicate first whether that number was higher or lower than the value of the quantity … these arbitrary numbers had a marked effect on estimates." | Optional: "a number from a wheel of fortune" is more exact than "a random number". |
| 2 | Introduction ¶1 | northcraft1987 | Anchoring with informative anchors, with experts and lay people, in property valuation | SUPPORTED | Abstract: "students and real estate agents toured and made pricing decisions about real estate properties … manipulated listing prices would anchor values assigned to the properties." | – |
| 3 | Introduction ¶1 | englich2006 | Anchoring with arbitrary anchors, with experts, in criminal sentencing | SUPPORTED | Abstract: "sentencing decisions of experienced legal professionals are influenced by irrelevant sentencing demands even if they are blatantly determined at random … throwing dice (Study 3)." | – |
| 4 | Introduction ¶1 | furnham2011 | Review evidence for the whole sentence (arbitrary/informative anchors, experts, property, sentencing) | SUPPORTED | p. 39 (OCR): "car experts … property values (Northcraft and Neale, 1987) and experienced legal professionals … were significantly influenced by irrelevant anchors on their sentencing"; "irrelevant anchors produce …". | – |
| 5 | Introduction ¶1 | roseler2022meta | Meta-analysis of OpAQ data from 90 studies; pooled *g* = 0.69 | SUPPORTED | p. 18: "m = 90 independent studies with a total sample size of N = 17,708"; abstract: "g = 0.689, 95% CI [0.589, 0.789] … k = 393". | – |
| 6 | Introduction ¶1 | roseler2022opaq | Source of the openly shared trial-level data | SUPPORTED | Data paper: "Each row in the dataset represents one trial". The data paper reports 96 studies; the 90 refers to the meta-analysis subset. | – |
| 7 | Evidence on extremity ¶1 | chapman1994 | Direct quote "implausibly extreme anchors had a proportionally smaller effect than anchors close to the expected value", in lottery valuations | SUPPORTED (abstract only) | Abstract, p. 223: "In Experiments 1 and 2, implausibly extreme anchors had a proportionally smaller effect than anchors close to the expected value of the lotteries evaluated." The quoted words are verbatim; the source sentence continues "of the lotteries evaluated". | Add a page number for the quote (p. 223). |
| 8 | Evidence on extremity ¶1 | strack1997 | Implausible anchors produced a **larger raw shift** in estimates than plausible ones | PARTLY | Study 3 analysed z-standardised estimates, not raw values (Table 6: plausible .04 / −.13; implausible .25 / −.17). The Anchor × Plausibility interaction was not significant, F(1, 66) = 3.55, p < .07; authors: "plausibility yielded no significant effect … implausible anchors were at least as effective as plausible ones" (p. 442–443). | "@strack1997 found that implausible anchors were at least as effective as plausible ones (in standardised estimates; the difference was not significant)." |
| 9 | Evidence on extremity ¶1 | mussweiler2001 | Estimates under implausible anchors far beyond the plausible range were **no higher than** under a plausible high anchor | PARTLY | The authors' test compares the two implausible high anchors with each other: Study 1 (700 vs 900 °C) t(29) = .2; Study 2 (214 vs 271 years) t(53) = .62; abstract: "implausible anchors that differ extremely produce similar absolute estimates." They did not test implausible vs plausible high. Study 1 means fit the claim (−23.27, −24.44 vs plausible high −24.84), but in Study 2 both implausible means were numerically higher than the plausible high mean (72.86 and 75.26 vs 70.36; Table 2, p. 156). | "Two implausible high anchors that differed greatly (e.g., 214 vs 271 years for Gandhi's age at death) produced similar estimates [@mussweiler2001]." |
| 10 | Evidence on extremity ¶1 | wegener2001 | Very extreme anchors had smaller effects than moderate ones | SUPPORTED | Abstract: "three separate data collections show that extreme anchors can have less influence on judgments than more moderate anchors." Exp. 1B z-means: moderate +.52/−.41 vs very extreme +.15/−.25 (p. 65). | – |
| 11 | Evidence on extremity ¶1 | imhoff2023 | Study 2: dot patterns of ~500 dots, standards labelled with exact dot count, up to 400 dots from target in 20-dot steps; pull levelled off beyond ~300 dots | SUPPORTED | p. 9: "estimate 41 dot patterns of around 500 dots (±10 dots) next to standards that varied between 400 dots above or below the target image in intervals of 20 dots"; standards labelled "This image contains [between 93 and 901] dots". p. 10: estimates "increased as the standards became more removed up until a difference of around 300 dots was reached, after which estimates remained stable". Estimates were z-transformed within participant. "Most fine-grained test so far" is the manuscript's own judgement. | – |
| 12 | Evidence on extremity ¶2 | roseler2022meta | Hedges' *g* increased with relative anchor–true-value distance; concluded against the prediction that extreme anchors produce smaller effects | SUPPORTED | Table 2 (p. 21): relative distance b = 0.040, k = 312, p < .001. p. 30: "The Selective Accessibility Model's prediction that extreme anchors can lead to smaller (or even negative) effects was not supported. Instead, anchoring extremeness was related in a nonlinear but positive way". | – |
| 13 | Evidence on extremity ¶2 | schley2026 | Extremity coded as a binary flag for anchors the original authors described as extreme; no difference in effect size | PARTLY (minor) | Coding table: "whether study conditions used extreme or otherwise implausible anchors … original authors defined the anchor as 'extreme' or 'implausible', or when there were other anchor levels that were more moderate" (coders also classified, e.g., O'Conor et al. 1999). Result: "little evidence (βs −0.02 to 0.09) of extreme anchors influencing the effect size". | "…coded extremity as a binary flag, mainly for anchors that the original authors described as extreme or implausible, and found no difference…" |
| 14 | Evidence on extremity ¶2 | barrera2024 | Anchored mean = weighted average of anchor and crowd mean; weight decays exponentially with anchor–truth distance; weight fell with distance across 30 percentage questions | SUPPORTED | Eq. 4: w = w0·e^(−β\|A−θ\|); "the anchored mean … is a weighted average of the anchor and the mean of the original distribution of values µ"; Exp. 2 used "30 general-knowledge questions that involved the estimation of a percentage", anchors fixed at 5% and 95%; r = −0.56 between weight and distance; exponential fit better than linear or hyperbolic. Distance varied across questions, not within. | – |
| 15 | Evidence on extremity ¶3 | jacowitz1995 | Anchoring index = difference between median estimates under high and low anchors divided by the difference between anchors | SUPPORTED | p. 1162: "AI = [Median(high anchor) − Median(low anchor)] / [High anchor − Low anchor]". | – |
| 16 | Evidence on extremity ¶3 | roseler2022meta | Called for a unitless measure; quote "to formalize the relationship between anchor distance and adjustment strength" | SUPPORTED (quote verbatim) | p. 34: "the relative strength of adjustment could be used because it provides a unitless and general metric. Standardized measures could help to formalize the relationship between anchor distance and adjustment strength as has been done in similar fields". In the source, the grammatical subject of the quoted phrase is "Standardized measures", and the call is phrased as a suggestion. | Optional: "suggested that relative adjustment, a unitless measure, could help 'to formalize … strength' (p. 34)". Add the page number. |
| 17 | Process models, M1 | lieder2018a | Adjustment formalised as a Metropolis-Hastings chain starting at the anchor and moving towards the belief distribution | SUPPORTED | "Metropolis-Hastings algorithm … given an initial guess x̂0, which we will assume to be the anchor a … the distribution of estimates Q(x̂t) converges to the posterior distribution P(X\|K)". | – |
| 18 | Process models, M1 ("Lieder et al.", no key) | lieder2018a | Geometric-convergence approximation implies constant proportional pull (their Eq. 4) | SUPPORTED | Eq. 3 bounds bias by (a − x)·r^t; "assuming that the bound is tight … E[x̂t\|x,a] ≈ a·r^t + (1 − r^t)·x. (4)". Eq. 4 has the same number in the preprint and the published version. The statements that the approximation holds only near the belief and that a fixed number of steps gives a rising pull are the manuscript's own reasoning, not Lieder et al.'s. | Optional: mark the "holds for anchors near the belief" statement as the authors' own result (e.g., "in our simulations"). |
| 19 | Process models, M1R | lieder2018a, Eq. 2 | Number of adjustments minimises expected error plus a time cost per adjustment | SUPPORTED | Eq. 2: t* = argmin_t E[cost(x, x̂t) + γ·t], "γ is the time cost per adjustment". | – |
| 20 | Process models, M1R (same paragraph) | lieder2018a | Anchors in the plausible range are barely adjusted, far anchors get many adjustments; the pull can fall with extremity; shape depends on time cost | SUPPORTED (figure, not text) | Fig. 4a: at time costs above about 10⁻², zero adjustments for anchors 0–1σ from the posterior mean and more for 3–5σ; Fig. 4b: the bias after the optimal number of adjustments grows less than proportionally with distance and depends on time cost. The text does not state this in words. | Optional: "(their Fig. 4)". |
| 21 | Process models, M2 | turner2016 | Constant-weight integration is the simplest version of the anchor integration model | SUPPORTED | Basic AIM: normal prior × normal information function centred on the anchor with fixed κ, combined by Bayes' rule (Eq. 1), which gives a precision-weighted average of prior mean and anchor. The log-unit specification is the manuscript's own. | – |
| 22 | Process models, M3 | epley2006 | People accept anchors inside the plausible range and adjust from implausible anchors only to the edge of that range | PARTLY | E&G formulate this for **self-generated** anchors: "adjustments from self-generated anchor values tend to be insufficient because they terminate once a plausible value is reached"; "the present account applies only to adjustment-based anchoring effects and not accessibility-based anchoring effects". They predicted and found that estimates for experimenter-provided anchors are *not* skewed within the plausible range (Study 1a). The manuscript applies M3 to provided anchors. | Add @mussweiler2001 for provided anchors ("judges may adjust from an implausible anchor until a plausible value for the target is reached", abstract), and state that @epley2006 proposed the stopping rule for self-generated anchors. |
| 23 | Process models, M4 | wegener2001 | Proposal that extreme anchors lose influence because they are implausible | SUPPORTED | Title "Anchor Plausibility and the Limits of Anchor Effectiveness"; Exp. 2 mediation: when rated plausibility was entered, "the Extremity effect was diminished and even reversed" (p. 66). | – |
| 24 | Process models, M4 | turner2016 | In AIM, an anchor's influence depends on its consistency with prior beliefs | SUPPORTED | Sec. 5.2 "Prior consistency"; p. 24: "as an anchor becomes more inconsistent with a participant's information (i.e., becomes more implausible), our AIM assumes that the anchor will have a proportionally smaller influence". | – |
| 25 | Process models, M4 | strack1997 | Selective accessibility: anchoring arises from anchor-consistent knowledge activated during the comparison | SUPPORTED | Title "Explaining the enigmatic anchoring effect: Mechanisms of selective accessibility"; comparative task makes target knowledge accessible. | – |
| 26 | Process models, M4 | mussweiler1999 | Same as #25 | SUPPORTED | Abstract: "Applying this strategy selectively increases the accessibility of anchor-consistent knowledge which is then used to generate the subsequent absolute judgment." | – |
| 27 | Process models, M4 | roseler2022meta | Selective-accessibility accounts have been read as predicting smaller effects for implausible anchors | SUPPORTED | p. 5: "based on the Selective Accessibility Model, anchors that are too high or too low should lead to smaller anchoring effects (i.e., an inverted u-shaped relationship …)"; p. 11: extreme primes "can be excluded … and thus lead to contrast effects". R&S say "extreme", not "implausible". | – |
| 28 | Process models, after Fig. 1 ("Lieder et al.") | lieder2018a | Derived that bias grows linearly with distance when the number of adjustments is fixed | SUPPORTED | "the anchoring bias remaining after a fixed number of adjustments increases linearly with the distance from the anchor to the correct value". | – |
| 29 | Same sentence | lieder2018a | Showed how the optimal number of adjustments depends on distance | SUPPORTED | Fig. 4a (optimal number of adjustments by time cost and distance from anchor). | – |
| 30 | Same sentence | lieder2018a | "did not test how the anchoring index varies with extremity" | PARTLY | Lieder et al. simulated Russo & Schoemaker (1989), with anchors 500–1300 in steps of 200, and ran an MTurk replication (N = 300): "both Russo and Shoemaker's data and our replication confirm our model's qualitative prediction that the magnitude of the anchoring bias increases linearly with the anchor". A linear increase is a test of constant proportional influence across five levels. They did not model implausibly extreme anchors; they cite Chapman & Johnson (1994) for the limit of the linear increase. | "…and fitted their model to five anchor levels from Russo and Schoemaker (1989), where bias rose linearly with the anchor, but did not examine whether proportional influence changes for implausibly extreme anchors." |
| 31 | Same paragraph | turner2016 | Built an inverted U between extremity and **anchor influence** into the model "for simplicity" | PARTLY (minor) | p. 23: "For simplicity, AIM assumes that as the distance between the prior representation and the anchor increases, the anchor provides a marginally decreasing influence on the posterior representation, producing an inverted U-shaped relationship between anchor extremity and the magnitude of the shift from prior to posterior representation." The quote is correct. The inverted U is in the size of the shift; the anchor's influence parameter itself declines. It is part of the within-participant extension (Sec. 5), not the basic model. | "…built an inverted U between anchor extremity and the size of the shift in estimates into their model 'for simplicity'…" |
| 32 | Same paragraph | turner2016 | Tested with one anchor per item | SUPPORTED | Exp. 1: "Questions 1, 3, and 5 used high anchors (3500 miles, 55 miles per hour, and 5 million people) whereas Questions 2, 4, and 6 used low anchors"; Exp. 2 used the same items and anchors. Extremity relative to each participant's prior still varied. | – |
| 33 | Present study | roseler2022opaq | OpAQ is an openly licensed collection of trial-level anchoring data | SUPPORTED | "3.6 License: CC-By Attribution 4.0 International"; "Each row in the dataset represents one trial". | – |
| 34 | Present study | imhoff2023 | Dot-estimation evidence (contrast with OpAQ general-knowledge items) | SUPPORTED | As #11. | – |
| 35 | Method, Transparency | vandenakker2021 | Preregistration followed the secondary-data template | SUPPORTED | Title: "Preregistration of secondary data analysis: A template and tutorial". | – |
| 36 | Method, Data | roseler2022opaq; opaqosf | OpAQ aggregates open and contributed datasets into one trial-level file with harmonised design codes; CC-BY 4.0; no identifiers beyond sex, age, nationality | SUPPORTED | "we aggregated all openly available anchoring datasets … supplemented these with datasets that we received from other researchers' publications and file-drawers"; "coding numerous design features"; OSF osf.io/ygnvb; licence CC-BY 4.0; "do not contain identifying information". The file name `opaq_70a.csv` and its date are repository facts, not in the paper. | – |
| 37 | Method, Data (within-item set) | bahnik2021 | 13 general-knowledge items; each participant compared 13 random anchors between 1 and 1,000 to 13 **lengths and heights** | PARTLY (minor) | Abstract: "participants compared thirteen random anchors on the same scale to thirteen different objects"; p. 134–135: "The dimension of size was always specified to be length, height, or distance … The anchors therefore ranged from 1 to 1000". The OpAQ items include "distance of the subway tracks between stations". | "…to the lengths, heights and distances of 13 objects". Apply the same fix in Limitations (#50). |
| 38 | Method, Data (within-item set) | yoon2021 | Two items with **random** anchors | PARTLY | The two cells are Form C "Average price of a sofa bed at IKEA" and "Number of novels written by Stephen King" (design_cells.csv, OpAQ anchortype 1 = random). In Yoon et al.'s Appendix A, the anchors are the participant's own height and age: "A. How tall are you (in inches)? B. Think about whether the average price (in US dollars) of a sofa bed at IKEA is above or below the number you gave"; "A. How old are you? B. … more or less than the number of novels Stephen King has written". These are arbitrary numbers that participants supply, not random draws. The manuscript excludes "self-generated and incidental" anchors, and these are close to that category. | "…and two items from @yoon2021 whose anchors were participants' own height or age (coded as random in OpAQ)". The existing leave-one-study-out check (S2 without Yoon Form C) already covers this sensitivity. |
| 39 | Method, Data (within-item set) | imhoff2023 [Study 2] | Cologne cathedral item with 20 anchor levels from a supplementary anchoring task in Study 2 | SUPPORTED, with a caveat | Article p. 9: "A small traditional anchoring task … was also included after the main task … described in detail in the additional materials available online." Supplement "Study 2b": "whether the Cologne cathedral was higher or lower than some random anchor ranging from 10 to 390 meters in 20 meter intervals" (= 20 levels). **Caveats:** (a) the authors call the anchor "random" (random assignment of a grid value), while the manuscript and OpAQ class it as fixed; (b) the authors report "a simple positive linear model best fit the data … all other polynomial terms p > .63" (0.62 m per m), and "the classical anchoring paradigm did not show the expected levelling off of the anchoring effect even for the most extreme anchors". | Describe the anchors as values randomly assigned from a 20-level grid (and say how this squares with the "fixed" class). Where the manuscript reports this item's negative log-scale curvature (Sensitivity; Discussion ¶1; Limitations), add that the original authors found a linear raw-scale relation with no levelling-off. The two results are compatible (linear raw ≠ constant log elasticity), but a reader checking the source will otherwise see a contradiction. |
| 40 | Method, H1 | bates2015; kuznetsova2017; rcore2026 | Software used (lme4, lmerTest with Satterthwaite df, R) | SUPPORTED | Standard software citations; lmerTest provides Satterthwaite df. | – |
| 41 | Method, decision rules | lakens2017 | Justification of equivalence bounds (±0.05 for ρ) placed below the predictive intervals of M1, M3, M4 | PARTLY (minor) | Lakens is a primer on equivalence testing (TOST). It recommends bounds from the smallest effect size of interest and notes that equivalence tests "will likely stimulate researchers to specify which effect sizes are predicted by a theory". It does not cover deriving bounds from model predictive intervals. It concludes equivalence when the **90%** CI lies within the bounds. The manuscript uses 95% CIs (equivalent to TOST at α = .025, more conservative). | Cite for the procedure, not the bound values: "…classified as flat if the 95% CI for ρ lay within ±0.05 (an equivalence test at α = .025; @lakens2017)". The bound justification then rests on the model predictions. |
