| 43 | Method, Robustness | koenker1978; quantreg | Median regression; participant-cluster bootstrap | SUPPORTED | Regression quantiles; quantreg offers cluster bootstrap standard errors. | – |
| 44 | Method, Robustness; Results, Robustness | bahnik2021 | Identity of the study left out in R3 | SUPPORTED | OpAQ reference "Bahník, 2021a" = "Anchoring without scale distortion. JDM 16(1), 131" (6,578 estimates). | – |
| 45 | Results, Exploratory | roseler2022meta | Rising Hedges' *g* with extremity is "in line with" R&S | SUPPORTED | As #12. | – |
| 46 | Results, Sensitivity | imhoff2023 [Study 2] | Source of the single fixed-anchor item with 20 levels | SUPPORTED, with the caveat of #39 | See #39. The authors' own analysis of this item found no levelling-off. | See #39. |
| 47 | Discussion ¶2 | epley2006 | Adjustment that stops at the edge of the plausible range | PARTLY | As #22: proposed for self-generated anchors only. | Add @mussweiler2001; qualify @epley2006 as in #22. |
| 48 | Discussion ¶2 | wegener2001; turner2016 | Integration that discounts implausible anchors | SUPPORTED | As #23 and #24. | – |
| 49 | Discussion ¶2 | lieder2018a | Resource-rational agent invests more adjustments when the anchor is far off | SUPPORTED | Fig. 4a. In Lieder et al. the mechanism is error cost vs time cost, not plausibility as such, so the sentence's framing ("limited by how plausible it is") is the manuscript's interpretation. | Optional: "…limited by how implausible, or how far off, it is". |
| 50 | Discussion ¶2 | chapman1994; mussweiler2001; wegener2001 | Earlier experiments with few anchor levels in which implausible anchors had proportionally smaller effects | SUPPORTED | C&J abstract (#7); M&S: implausible anchors 18–72 SD from the mean gave estimates similar to a 1-SD anchor (#9); Wegener (#10). | – |
| 51 | Discussion ¶2 | barrera2024 | Distance-decaying anchoring weight | SUPPORTED | As #14. | – |
| 52 | Discussion ¶2 | imhoff2023 | Levelling-off of assimilation to symbolic anchors in dot estimation | SUPPORTED | As #11. The same paper's classic anchoring task (supplement Study 2b) did not level off (#39). | Optional: mention the contrast, since it bears on the claim. |
| 53 | Discussion ¶2 | mayer2024 | Dot-estimation task, anchors 35% or 70% from the true value; more distant anchors produced larger estimation errors | SUPPORTED | Exp. 1: anchors "either −70%, −35%, 35%, or 70% from the correct answer"; "a significant positive effect of anchor extremity emerged (β̂ = 4.88, 95% CI [2.80, 6.97] …), indicating more error and thus less accurate estimates for more inaccurate anchors". | – |
| 54 | Discussion ¶4 (across-cell) | roseler2022meta | Meta-analytic finding that larger anchor distances produce larger standardised effects | SUPPORTED | As #12. | – |
| 55 | Limitations ¶1 | bahnik2021 | 13 random anchors with 13 different lengths and heights | PARTLY (minor) | As #37 (also distances). The count of 6,578 estimates matches OpAQ. | "lengths, heights and distances". |
| 56 | Method, calibration; H3; Sensitivity | jacowitz1995 | AI for anchors at the 15th and 85th percentiles of unanchored estimates is about .49 | SUPPORTED | "anchors were respectively set at the 15th and 85th percentiles"; "Over the 15 problems, the overall mean of the AI is .49" (p. 1163–1164). ## Other observations (text without a citation key)

- **"Weber et al. (2021), whose item coding was questioned in a later correction"** (Results, Robustness) has no reference. The preregistration (line 76) identifies the source as a 2026 corrigendum to Weber & Röseler (2025). `roseler2024correction` in refs.bib (jopd.92) is **not** that correction: it only adds co-authors who were omitted from the OpAQ data paper ("was mistakenly published with the following co-authors omitted …"). Add a verified reference for the Weber & Röseler corrigendum, or describe the source in words.

Checked 2026-09-28 against the current `manuscript.qmd` (including the `@imhoff2023` and `@mayer2024` citations). Each row is one (sentence, key) pair. Verdicts: SUPPORTED / PARTLY / NOT SUPPORTED / COULD NOT CHECK. Reference existence was not re-checked.

Sources read (full text unless stated): Tversky & Kahneman 1974 (Science PDF); Northcraft & Neale 1987; Englich et al. 2006; Furnham & Boo 2011 (scanned PDF, OCR); Röseler & Schütz 2022 preprint (osf.io/wf2tn); OpAQ data paper (jopd.67) and its correction (jopd.92); Chapman & Johnson 1994 (**abstract only**, from the academia.edu record; the full text could not be obtained); Strack & Mussweiler 1997; Mussweiler & Strack 1999; Mussweiler & Strack 2001; Wegener et al. 2001; Schley & Weingarten manuscript version; Barrera-Lemarchand et al. 2024 (accepted manuscript); Jacowitz & Kahneman 1995 (scanned PDF, OCR); Lieder et al. 2018a (PsyArXiv preprint and eScholarship copy of the published version; equation numbers are the same in both); Turner & Schley 2016; Epley & Gilovich 2006; Bahník 2021; Yoon et al. 2021 (accepted manuscript incl. Appendix A); Imhoff & Barker 2023 (article + online supplement "Study 2b"); Mayer & Rebholz 2024 preprint; Lakens 2017 (preprint); van den Akker et al. 2021. For Bahník, Yoon, Frech and Imhoff items, the OpAQ file (`data/raw/opaq_70a.csv`) and `output/design_cells.csv` were also used to identify which items enter the analysis.

The subjects were instructed to indicate first whether that number was higher or lower than the value of the quantity … these arbitrary numbers had a marked effect on estimates." | Optional: "a number from a wheel of fortune" is more exact than "a random number". |
| 2 | Introduction ¶1 | northcraft1987 | Anchoring with informative anchors, with experts and lay people, in property valuation | SUPPORTED | Abstract: "students and real estate agents toured and made pricing decisions about real estate properties … manipulated listing prices would anchor values assigned to the properties." | – |
| 3 | Introduction ¶1 | englich2006 | Anchoring with arbitrary anchors, with experts, in criminal sentencing | SUPPORTED | Abstract: "sentencing decisions of experienced legal professionals are influenced by irrelevant sentencing demands even if they are blatantly determined at random … throwing dice (Study 3)." | – |
| 4 | Introduction ¶1 | furnham2011 | Review evidence for the whole sentence (arbitrary/informative anchors, experts, property, sentencing) | SUPPORTED | p. 39 (OCR): "car experts … property values (Northcraft and Neale, 1987) and experienced legal professionals … were significantly influenced by irrelevant anchors on their sentencing"; "irrelevant anchors produce …". | – |
| 5 | Introduction ¶1 | roseler2022meta | Meta-analysis of OpAQ data from 90 studies; pooled *g* = 0.69 | SUPPORTED | p. 18: "m = 90 independent studies with a total sample size of N = 17,708"; abstract: "g = 0.689, 95% CI [0.589, 0.789] … k = 393". | – |
| 6 | Introduction ¶1 | roseler2022opaq | Source of the openly shared trial-level data | SUPPORTED | Data paper: "Each row in the dataset represents one trial". The data paper reports 96 studies; the 90 refers to the meta-analysis subset. | – |
| 7 | Evidence on extremity ¶1 | chapman1994 | Direct quote "implausibly extreme anchors had a proportionally smaller effect than anchors close to the expected value", in lottery valuations | SUPPORTED (abstract only) | Abstract, p. 223: "In Experiments 1 and 2, implausibly extreme anchors had a proportionally smaller effect than anchors close to the expected value of the lotteries evaluated." The Anchor × Plausibility interaction was not significant, F(1, 66) = 3.55, p < .07; authors: "plausibility yielded no significant effect … implausible anchors were at least as effective as plausible ones" (p. 442–443). | "@strack1997 found that implausible anchors were at least as effective as plausible ones (in standardised estimates; the difference was not significant)." |

They did not test implausible vs plausible high. Study 1 means fit the claim (−23.27, −24.44 vs plausible high −24.84), but in Study 2 both implausible means were numerically higher than the plausible high mean (72.86 and 75.26 vs 70.36; Table 2, p. 156). | "Two implausible high anchors that differed greatly (e.g., 214 vs 271 years for Gandhi's age at death) produced similar estimates [@mussweiler2001]." |
| 10 | Evidence on extremity ¶1 | wegener2001 | Very extreme anchors had smaller effects than moderate ones | SUPPORTED | Abstract: "three separate data collections show that extreme anchors can have less influence on judgments than more moderate anchors." Distance varied across questions, not within. | – |
| 15 | Evidence on extremity ¶3 | jacowitz1995 | Anchoring index = difference between median estimates under high and low anchors divided by the difference between anchors | SUPPORTED | p. 1162: "AI = [Median(high anchor) − Median(low anchor)] / [High anchor − Low anchor]". | – |
| 16 | Evidence on extremity ¶3 | roseler2022meta | Called for a unitless measure; quote "to formalize the relationship between anchor distance and adjustment strength" | SUPPORTED (quote verbatim) | p. 34: "the relative strength of adjustment could be used because it provides a unitless and general metric. Standardized measures could help to formalize the relationship between anchor distance and adjustment strength as has been done in similar fields". In the source, the grammatical subject of the quoted phrase is "Standardized measures", and the call is phrased as a suggestion. | Optional: "suggested that relative adjustment, a unitless measure, could help 'to formalize … strength' (p. 34)". Add the page number. |
| 17 | Process models, M1 | lieder2018a | Adjustment formalised as a Metropolis-Hastings chain starting at the anchor and moving towards the belief distribution | SUPPORTED | "Metropolis-Hastings algorithm … given an initial guess x̂0, which we will assume to be the anchor a … the distribution of estimates Q(x̂t) converges to the posterior distribution P(X\|K)". | – |
| 18 | Process models, M1 ("Lieder et al.", no key) | lieder2018a | Geometric-convergence approximation implies constant proportional pull (their Eq. 4) | SUPPORTED | Eq. 3 bounds bias by (a − x)·r^t; "assuming that the bound is tight … E[x̂t\|x,a] ≈ a·r^t + (1 − r^t)·x. (4)". Eq. 4 has the same number in the preprint and the published version. The statements that the approximation holds only near the belief and that a fixed number of steps gives a rising pull are the manuscript's own reasoning, not Lieder et al.'s. | Optional: mark the "holds for anchors near the belief" statement as the authors' own result (e.g., "in our simulations"). |
| 19 | Process models, M1R | lieder2018a, Eq. 2 | Number of adjustments minimises expected error plus a time cost per adjustment | SUPPORTED | Eq. 2: t* = argmin_t E[cost(x, x̂t) + γ·t], "γ is the time cost per adjustment". | – |
| 20 | Process models, M1R (same paragraph) | lieder2018a | Anchors in the plausible range are barely adjusted, far anchors get many adjustments; the pull can fall with extremity; shape depends on time cost | SUPPORTED (figure, not text) | Fig. 4a: at time costs above about 10⁻², zero adjustments for anchors 0–1σ from the posterior mean and more for 3–5σ; Fig. 4b: the bias after the optimal number of adjustments grows less than proportionally with distance and depends on time cost. The text does not state this in words. | Optional: "(their Fig. 4)". |
| 21 | Process models, M2 | turner2016 | Constant-weight integration is the simplest version of the anchor integration model | SUPPORTED | Basic AIM: normal prior × normal information function centred on the anchor with fixed κ, combined by Bayes' rule (Eq. 1), which gives a precision-weighted average of prior mean and anchor. The log-unit specification is the manuscript's own. | – |
| 22 | Process models, M3 | epley2006 | People accept anchors inside the plausible range and adjust from implausible anchors only to the edge of that range | PARTLY | E&G formulate this for **self-generated** anchors: "adjustments from self-generated anchor values tend to be insufficient because they terminate once a plausible value is reached"; "the present account applies only to adjustment-based anchoring effects and not accessibility-based anchoring effects". The manuscript applies M3 to provided anchors. | Add @mussweiler2001 for provided anchors ("judges may adjust from an implausible anchor until a plausible value for the target is reached", abstract), and state that @epley2006 proposed the stopping rule for self-generated anchors. |

5 @bahnik2021    2 @barrera2024    1 @bates2015    2 @chapman1994    1 @englich2006    2 @epley2006    5 @fig    1 @furnham2011    1 @gmail    6 @imhoff2023    2 @jacowitz1995    1 @koenker1978    1 @kuznetsova2017    1 @lakens2017    3 @lieder2018a    1 @mayer2024    1 @mussweiler1999    2 @mussweiler2001    1 @northcraft1987    2 @opaqosf    1 @quantreg    1 @rcore2026    6 @roseler2022meta    3 @roseler2022opaq    1 @schley2026    2 @strack1997    3 @tbl    4 @turner2016    1 @tversky1974    1 @vandenakker2021    1 @viechtbauer2010    4 @wegener2001    1 @yoon2021 
Numeric judgements are drawn towards numbers people have just considered. In the classic demonstration, participants who first judged whether the percentage of African countries in the United Nations was higher or lower than a random number gave estimates that moved towards that number [@tversky1974]. The effect appears with arbitrary and informative anchors, with lay people and experts, and in consequential settings such as property valuation and criminal sentencing [@northcraft1987; @englich2006; @furnham2011]. A meta-analysis of openly shared trial-level data from 90 anchoring studies estimated a pooled standardised effect of *g* = 0.69 [@roseler2022meta; @roseler2022opaq].
Experiments that varied anchor extremity have produced mixed results. @chapman1994 found that "implausibly extreme anchors had a proportionally smaller effect than anchors close to the expected value" in lottery valuations. @strack1997 found that implausible anchors produced a larger raw shift in estimates than plausible ones. When implausible anchors were placed far beyond the plausible range, estimates under them were no higher than estimates under a plausible high anchor [@mussweiler2001], and @wegener2001 found that very extreme anchors had smaller effects than moderate ones. These studies compared two to four anchor levels, mostly for a handful of items. The most fine-grained test so far used a perceptual task: @imhoff2023 [Study 2] showed participants dot patterns of about 500 dots next to standards labelled with their exact number of dots, which differed from the target by up to 400 dots in 20-dot steps. Estimates were drawn towards these symbolic anchors, but the pull levelled off once the anchor differed from the target by more than about 300 dots.
The two recent meta-analyses reach different conclusions. Using the Open Anchoring Quest (OpAQ) data, @roseler2022meta found that Hedges' *g* increased with the relative distance between anchor and true value and concluded against the prediction that extreme anchors produce smaller effects. @schley2026 coded extremity as a binary flag for anchors that the original authors described as extreme and found no difference in effect size. @barrera2024 modelled the anchored crowd mean as a weighted average of anchor and crowd mean, with a weight that decays exponentially with the distance between anchor and truth, and found that this weight fell with distance across 30 percentage questions.
These results are hard to compare because they measure anchor influence in different units. A standardised mean difference between high- and low-anchor conditions rises with the distance between the anchors even if every anchor pulls estimates by the same proportion of its distance. A finding that *g* grows with anchor distance is therefore compatible with constant, rising and falling proportional influence. The theories speak to the proportional pull: how much of the distance between belief and anchor is carried into the estimate. @jacowitz1995 captured this with the anchoring index, the difference between median estimates under high and low anchors divided by the difference between the anchors, and @roseler2022meta called for such a unitless measure "to formalize the relationship between anchor distance and adjustment strength".
In *adjustment to the plausible boundary* (M3), people accept anchors that lie inside the range of values they find plausible and adjust from implausible anchors only until they reach the edge of that range [@epley2006]. Beyond the boundary the estimate stops moving, so the proportional pull falls towards zero.
In *plausibility-discounted integration* (M4), the anchor's weight declines as the anchor becomes implausible. This formalises the proposal that extreme anchors lose influence because they are implausible [@wegener2001], and it resembles the anchor integration model, in which an anchor's influence depends on how consistent it is with prior beliefs [@turner2016]. Selective-accessibility accounts, in which anchoring arises from anchor-consistent knowledge activated during the comparison [@strack1997; @mussweiler1999], have been read as predicting smaller effects for implausible anchors [@roseler2022meta]. The pull falls, and far enough out, a more extreme anchor moves the estimate back towards the belief.
The models also include a no-anchoring baseline (M0). Lieder et al. derived that bias grows linearly with anchor distance when the number of adjustments is fixed and showed how the optimal number of adjustments depends on distance, but did not test how the anchoring index varies with extremity. @turner2016 built an inverted U between extremity and anchor influence into their model "for simplicity" and tested it with one anchor per item.
OpAQ [@roseler2022opaq; @opaqosf] aggregates openly available and contributed anchoring datasets into one trial-level file with harmonised design codes. We used the newest version of the file (`opaq_70a.csv`, dated 10 February 2023), which contains `r nf(dc$opaq_rows)` estimates from `r dc$opaq_studies` studies and `r dc$opaq_items` items. It is licensed under CC-BY 4.0 and contains no personal identifiers beyond sex, age and nationality, none of which we used.
- **Within-item set** (primary): item-study cells with at least three distinct anchor values. It contains `r dc$within_cells` cells from `r dc$within_studies` studies (`r nf(dc$within_rows)` estimates, `r nf(dc$within_participants)` participants). Fifteen cells used random anchors: 13 general-knowledge items from @bahnik2021, in which each participant compared 13 random anchors between 1 and 1,000 to 13 lengths and heights, and two items from @yoon2021. Five cells used fixed anchors: four items with 10 high anchor levels each from unpublished data by Frech et al. (2021), contributed to OpAQ, and one item (the height of Cologne cathedral) with 20 anchor levels from a supplementary anchoring task in @imhoff2023 [Study 2].
- **Across-cell set** (secondary): cells with fixed or relevant anchors, exactly one low and one high anchor value, a log ratio of at least 0.25 between them, and at least 10 estimates per anchor. It contains `r dc$across_cells` cells from `r dc$across_studies` studies (`r nf(dc$across_rows)` estimates).

[@tbl-cells] describes the within-item cells. OpAQ labels two of the source studies differently from their publications: "Bahník, 2021a" is @bahnik2021, and "Imhoff & Barker, 2022, Study 2" is a supplementary task in @imhoff2023.
**Decision rules.** The shape test was interpreted only if the confidence interval for *b* lay above zero (gate G1). We then classified the curvature, in this order, as *flat* if the confidence interval for ρ lay within the equivalence bounds ±0.05, as *rising* if the interval for *g* lay above zero, as *falling* if it lay below zero, and otherwise as inconclusive. The bounds sit just below the smallest relative curvature in the 95% predictive interval of M1, M3 and M4 and far outside that of M2 [@lakens2017]. Applied to the simulated replicates, this rule labelled data generated by M1 as rising in more than 99% of replicates, data from M3 and M4 as falling in more than 99%, data from M2 as flat in more than 99%, and data from M0 as failing the gate in all replicates.
The within-item result held in the preregistered robustness analyses that retained the random-anchor data. Median regression without the gross-error rule gave *g* = `r f3(r_("R1_median_regression_g"))`, `r ci(r_("R1_median_regression_g", "lo"), r_("R1_median_regression_g", "hi"))`. Replacing the curvature term by separate slopes for near and far anchors showed that the slope for anchors more than one log unit from the true value differed from the slope near the true value by `r f2(r_("R2_far_minus_near_slope"))`, `r ci(r_("R2_far_minus_near_slope", "lo"), r_("R2_far_minus_near_slope", "hi"), 2)`. Without @bahnik2021 the estimate was similar but very imprecise, *g* = `r f3(r_("R3_without_bahnik_g"))`, `r ci(r_("R3_without_bahnik_g", "lo"), r_("R3_without_bahnik_g", "hi"), 2)`.
*Dependence on single studies (H1).* Leaving out any one of the three smaller studies left the curvature negative with confidence intervals excluding zero (*g* from `r f3(min(s_("S2_without_Frech et al., 2021"), s_("S2_without_Yoon et al., 2021, Form C"), s_("S2_without_Imhoff & Barker, 2022, Study 2")))` to `r f3(max(s_("S2_without_Frech et al., 2021"), s_("S2_without_Yoon et al., 2021, Form C"), s_("S2_without_Imhoff & Barker, 2022, Study 2")))`). Adding study-level random effects gave *g* = `r f3(s_("S2_study_random_effect"))`, `r ci(s_("S2_study_random_effect", "lo"), s_("S2_study_random_effect", "hi"))`. The single fixed-anchor item with 20 anchor levels [the supplementary task of @imhoff2023, Study 2] showed a negative curvature on its own, *g* = `r f3(s_("S2_imhoff_barker_only"))`, `r ci(s_("S2_imhoff_barker_only", "lo"), s_("S2_imhoff_barker_only", "hi"))`.
The negative curvature contradicts two simple accounts. Anchor-and-adjust with a fixed number of steps predicts that far anchors keep more of their distance, because a bounded number of bounded steps cannot correct a large gap; the data show the reverse. Constant-weight integration, the simplest version of the anchor integration model, predicts no change in proportional pull; it too is contradicted. The accounts that predict a decline share one feature: the anchor's influence is limited by how plausible it is. This holds for adjustment that stops at the edge of the plausible range [@epley2006], for integration that discounts implausible anchors [@wegener2001; @turner2016], and for a resource-rational agent who invests more adjustments when the anchor is far off [@lieder2018a]. The result fits earlier experiments with few anchor levels in which implausible anchors had proportionally smaller effects [@chapman1994; @mussweiler2001; @wegener2001], the distance-decaying anchoring weight of @barrera2024, and the levelling-off of assimilation to symbolic anchors in dot estimation [@imhoff2023]. It extends these findings to general-knowledge magnitudes, to anchors far outside the plausible range, and to a proportional outcome. In a dot-estimation task with anchors 35% or 70% away from the true value, the more distant anchors produced larger estimation errors [@mayer2024]; a larger absolute effect is compatible with a declining proportional pull, so the two findings do not conflict.
The primary evidence rests largely on one study. Thirteen of the 20 within-item cells, and `r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * 6578 / dc$within_rows)` of the within-item estimates, come from @bahnik2021, in which participants compared 13 random anchors with 13 different lengths and heights. Without this study the within-item curvature had the same sign but a confidence interval too wide to be informative. The random anchors also differ from the fixed anchors that dominate applied settings. The preregistered test of the fixed-anchor stratum was not informative; in an exploratory analysis, the one fixed-anchor item with 20 anchor levels showed the same decline, but it is a single item. A direct test of the extremity function for informative anchors needs experiments that present many anchor levels for many items.

content.text:
The full table (57 claim–citation pairs) is in `~/Documents/Coding/ai-jdm-paper/manuscript/citation_check.md`. I did not edit the manuscript. It changed on disk while I was checking, so I re-checked the table against the current `manuscript.qmd`, including the new `@imhoff2023` and `@mayer2024` citations. **No citation is NOT SUPPORTED. 12 are PARTLY**, all listed below. None is COULD NOT CHECK, but Chapman & Johnson (1994) could only be checked against its abstract.

**Three problems that affect the analysis story, not just wording**

1. **Yoon et al. (2021): the "random anchors" were not random** (Method, Data, within-item set). The two cells are the price of a sofa bed at IKEA and the number of Stephen King novels. In Yoon et al.'s Appendix A, participants first give their own height in inches or their own age, and that number is the anchor. OpAQ codes these as random, but the manuscript excludes self-generated and incidental anchors, and these are close to that category.
   - *Fix:* "two items from @yoon2021 whose anchors were participants' own height or age (coded as random in OpAQ)".
2. **Imhoff & Barker (2023), Cologne cathedral item** (Method, Data; Sensitivity; Discussion; Limitations). The item and its 20 anchor levels are confirmed (supplement "Study 2b": 10–390 m in 20 m steps). Two points conflict with how the manuscript uses it:
   - The authors call these "some random anchor", but the manuscript counts the item as fixed.
   - The authors found a straight-line fit ("all other polynomial terms p > .63"). They state it "did not show the expected levelling off … even for the most extreme anchors". The manuscript reports a negative curvature for this item on the log scale. The two results are compatible, but a reader who checks the source will see a contradiction.
   - *Fix:* say how the anchors were assigned, and report the authors' raw-scale result next to the log-scale curvature.
3. **Epley & Gilovich (2006) is the wrong sole source for the plausible-boundary model** (model M3 and Discussion ¶2). They proposed the stopping rule only for self-generated anchors: "the present account applies only to adjustment-based anchoring effects and not accessibility-based anchoring effects". Their data showed that estimates after experimenter-provided anchors are not skewed towards the anchor side of the plausible range.
   - *Fix:* also cite @mussweiler2001 ("judges may adjust from an implausible anchor until a plausible value for the target is reached"), and state that E&G's version is for self-generated anchors.

**Other PARTLY items**

- **Strack & Mussweiler (1997)** (Evidence on extremity). "Implausible anchors produced a larger raw shift" is not what the authors report. Their analysis used standardised estimates, and the difference was not significant (interaction p < .07): implausible anchors were "at least as effective as plausible ones". The raw per-item means in their Appendix do show a larger difference in 7 of 8 items, but the authors neither report nor test this.
  - *Fix:* "found that implausible anchors were at least as effective as plausible ones (standardised estimates; difference not significant)".
- **Mussweiler & Strack (2001)** (Evidence on extremity). "Estimates … were no higher than under a plausible high anchor" was not tested by the authors. In both studies the implausible-anchor means are slightly higher than the plausible-high mean: −24.44 and −23.27 vs −24.84 °C; 72.86 and 75.26 vs 70.36 years. Their actual finding is that two very different implausible anchors produced similar estimates.
  - *Fix:* "Two implausible high anchors that differed greatly (e.g., 214 vs 271 years for Gandhi's age at death) produced similar estimates."
- **Schley & Weingarten (2026)** (Evidence on extremity). Their binary flag also covered anchors described as "implausible" and cases the coders judged extreme themselves. I checked the manuscript version, not the published article.
  - *Fix:* "mainly for anchors the original authors described as extreme or implausible".
- **Lieder et al. (2018a)** (Process models, after Fig. 1). "Did not test how the anchoring index varies with extremity" is too strong. They fitted Russo & Schoemaker's five anchor levels and ran a replication with 300 participants, finding that bias rose linearly with the anchor.
  - *Fix:* "…fitted five anchor levels from Russo and Schoemaker (1989), where bias rose linearly, but did not examine whether proportional influence changes for implausibly extreme anchors."
- **Turner & Schley (2016)** (same paragraph). The "for simplicity" quote is verbatim. Their inverted U is between extremity and "the magnitude of the shift" in estimates. The anchor's influence itself declines with extremity.
  - *Fix:* "an inverted U between anchor extremity and the size of the shift in estimates".
- **Bahník (2021)** (Method, Data; Limitations). The objects were lengths, heights *and distances* ("The dimension of size was always specified to be length, height, or distance").
  - *Fix:* "lengths, heights and distances", in both places.
- **Lakens (2017)** (Decision rules). It supports equivalence testing in general, not deriving the ±0.05 bounds from model predictions. Lakens uses 90% confidence intervals; the manuscript's 95% intervals correspond to an equivalence test at α = .025.
  - *Fix:* cite Lakens for the procedure ("an equivalence test at α = .025; @lakens2017") and let the model predictions justify the bounds.

**Two further items you need to know about**

- **Chapman & Johnson (1994) was checked against the abstract only.** The full text was not available (Wiley paywall; only the academia.edu record). The quote is verbatim from the abstract, where the sentence continues "…of the lotteries evaluated". Add p. 223 for the quote.
- **"Weber et al. (2021), whose item coding was questioned in a later correction" has no reference** (Results, Robustness). The preregistration names the source as a 2026 corrigendum to Weber & Röseler (2025). `roseler2024correction` (jopd.92) is not that source: it only adds co-authors who were left off the OpAQ data paper.
  - *Fix:* add a verified reference for the Weber & Röseler corrigendum, or describe the source in words.

**Checks that passed**

- Both direct quotes are verbatim: Chapman & Johnson, and Röseler & Schütz ("to formalize the relationship between anchor distance and adjustment strength", p. 34; add the page number).
- The numbers are correct: Röseler & Schütz report 90 studies and g = 0.689; Barrera-Lemarchand et al. used 30 percentage questions; Jacowitz & Kahneman report a mean index of .49 with anchors at the 15th and 85th percentiles.
- Lieder et al.'s Eq. 2 and Eq. 4 have the same numbers in the preprint and the published version.
- Tversky & Kahneman: the number came from a wheel of fortune. "A random number" is acceptable wording.
- Supported as cited: Mayer & Rebholz (2024), Imhoff & Barker's dot-estimation results, Wegener et al. (2001), Northcraft & Neale (1987), Englich et al. (2006), Furnham & Boo (2011), the OpAQ papers, van den Akker et al. (2021), and the software citations.

Source texts I extracted are in `/tmp/jdmsim/citecheck/`; downloaded PDFs are cached in `~/.claude/cache/pdfs/`.
